## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_Why can a robot recognize what to do yet still be too late to act?_

Learned models are what let a physical machine handle objects and scenes that no engineer enumerated, and they are also the largest and least predictable computation the machine carries. A model that recognizes the right object still has to move its weights through an onboard processor that sensing and control also depend on, and a larger model that recognizes more takes longer to answer. While it computes, the world keeps moving, so a correct answer can arrive after the conditions that justified it have changed. Predicting a sequence of future motions keeps the actuators supplied between model updates, but it cannot make those motions respond to observations the model has not yet received, and a proposal that arrives on time can still be wrong in ways the model's own confidence does not reveal. An engineer who treats the learned model as a function that returns actions cannot size the processor, set the rates at which proposals are renewed, or say how long the machine may keep moving on an answer that has gone stale. Because motion beyond the causal boundary cannot be recalled, every learned proposal must remain a request that an independent permission path can refuse in time.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Compare classical analytical pipelines and learned representations on coverage, sensory robustness, and formal verifiability
- Calculate the memory wall bound on a model's fresh-evaluation rate ($f \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth / \WeightMemoryWeights$) under the embodied batch size 1 constraint, and explain why weight-only quantization shortens the bandwidth-bound decode but not the compute-bound prefill
- Estimate key-value cache expansion from multi-camera tokenization, hidden dimensions, and retained history windows
- Explain how action chunking ($\Horizon$) amortizes off-chip weight transfers over physical wall-clock time without improving closed-loop reaction latency
- Compare autoregressive, one-pass, and iterative action decoders by the sequential evaluations and off-chip transfers one chunk costs
- Apply replanning period, inference latency, and target drift to size an action chunk for a dynamic target
- Evaluate the interface between a slow and a fast proposer by what the permission path can check against its own evidence
- Diagnose cognitive failure modes: semantic hallucinations, uncalibrated softmax overconfidence, perceptual chattering, and expired intent leases
- Identify the trajectory, timestamps, and validity information a proposer must hand to independent real-time verification

:::

## The Embodied Brain {#sec-brain-embodied}

The body's limit records tell the permission path what it must refuse, but they cannot say what the machine should do next. That choice belongs to the Brain, the deliberative layer that interprets incoming sensor telemetry and proposes what the physical body should execute next. Over the past decade, physical AI architectures have transitioned from hand-authored geometric pipelines and finite-state machines to learned models, notably vision-language-action (VLA) architectures that map natural language instructions and camera pixels directly to candidate end-effector motions for objects no engineer explicitly modeled. This shift places the machine's most computationally intensive workloads on its least predictable path. A deep neural proposer requires billions of operations, contends for shared memory bus bandwidth with low-latency sensing and control tasks, and predicts future actions for an environment that continues to evolve during inference. A fundamental physical constraint governs this interaction: a learned proposal remains useful only if it arrives, and remains physically valid, within the time window permitted by environmental dynamics. Furthermore, every candidate trajectory remains strictly a proposal. The hard-real-time permission path beneath the proposal boundary holds exclusive authority to validate and admit candidate motions before they actuate physical hardware.

The warehouse mobile manipulator illustrates this boundary concretely. The robot can operate within every torque, thermal, voltage, and braking limit of its body, and meet the freshness deadline that the body's budgets set for this same pick-station grasp, yet still fail to grasp an unfamiliar ceramic mug traveling along an active conveyor. Low-level limits safeguard physical actuators against structural and electrical damage, but they cannot identify the geometry of a graspable handle or plan an obstacle-free trajectory around a coworker's arm. A learned vision-action model supplies this missing perceptual interpretation. However, because neural network outputs carry no formal safety guarantees, every generated action sequence remains an unverified candidate until the permission path checks it against fresh telemetry and established safety envelopes.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The mobile manipulator's torque, thermal, voltage, and braking limits are established in @sec-body-five-budgets.
:::

This division exposes an inescapable timing dilemma: physical dynamics do not pause while inference runs. As the vision model evaluates sensory frames, the conveyor belt advances, and the manipulator must continue tracking previously admitted waypoints without stalling or jerking. Deploying a larger foundation model can enhance open-world object recognition, but the resulting inference latency delays subsequent updates. Systems architects must therefore decouple three distinct temporal quantities: the observation frequency at which the proposer ingests fresh sensor frames, the trajectory horizon spanning the future waypoints contained within each proposal, and the validity window over which those predictions remain physically accurate. Synthesizing longer action horizons can bridge execution between inference cycles, but generating additional waypoints does not refresh the perceptual evidence that produced them.

```{python}
#| label: brain-two-speed-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO-SPEED RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-two-speed-brain (fig03_two_speed_brain.svg) in the chapter
# │          opening.
# │ Goal:    Print the caption's rates and keep the SVG's hand-drawn labels
# │          equal to the running machine's registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz, 336 ms; chunk renewal 20 Hz, 40 ms inference;
# │          1 kHz permission tick.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, check

class TwoSpeedRates:
    """Registry rates that fig03_two_speed_brain.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: derived (prefill plus decode)
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws the intent model at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(round(t_intent.magnitude) == 336, f"SVG draws 336 ms per intent evaluation; registry says {t_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(t_chunk.magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws 40 ms chunk inference; registry says {t_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_tick.to(hertz).magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, f"SVG draws a 1 kHz permission tick; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_tick_str = fmt_frequency(f_tick, unit=ureg.kilohertz, precision=0)
```

The machine card of @sec-boundary-running-machine already commits the running machine to one answer, the **two-speed brain architecture**\index{Two-speed brain architecture!hybrid control}: a slow intent model revised at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_intent_str` above a fast chunk policy renewed at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_chunk_str`, both proposing to a permission path that checks measured state on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick (@fig-two-speed-brain). The card states these rates; this chapter derives them. The slow intent model names a target; the fast chunk policy emits an action chunk, the short sequence of future setpoints from one inference that @sec-boundary-prediction-to-action introduced, so the drives below have motion to track between evaluations [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Three claims carry the design, and the sections that follow test each one. No single large model can renew its proposal fast enough to supply the arm. A chunk keeps the arm supplied without keeping the evidence behind it fresh. Finally, the permission path can refuse the slow model's intent, and not only the fast model's motion, only if that intent arrives as a target it can compare with its own depth measurements and clock, which means a pose stamped with the capture time of the frame it came from (@sec-brain-proposer-interface).

::: {#fig-two-speed-brain fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two-speed brain architecture**: Above the proposal boundary, two learned proposers run at their own rates, an intent model at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_intent_str` and a chunk policy renewing at `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_chunk_str`. Below it, the permission path checks each proposal against measured state on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick, and the drives close their own current and velocity loops. A proposal carries no authority until it is admitted; a refusal returns the proposers to a plan from measured state." fig-alt="Two regions separated by a dashed vertical line labeled proposal boundary. Left region, Brain learned proposers: observations feed an intent model at 2 hertz and 336 milliseconds per evaluation, which passes a goal to a chunk policy at 20 hertz renewal and 40 milliseconds inference; a state resynchronization box below feeds the chunk policy. Right region, Nervous System and Body: encoders and scanner feed a permission path at a 1 kilohertz tick, which sends an admitted command to drives with current and velocity loops, which move the physical plant; the plant feeds back to the encoders. A dashed proposal arrow crosses from the chunk policy to the permission path, and a dashed refusal arrow returns from the permission path to state resynchronization."}
![](images/svg/fig03_two_speed_brain.svg){width="90%"}
:::

A learned proposer earns its place in an embodied system when training distribution coverage generalizes beyond preprogrammed edge cases. In the conveyor pick task, this capability translates into interpreting natural language instructions, recognizing the target mug amid visual clutter, and proposing reachable grasp affordances. However, high-level semantic identification alone cannot direct a robot arm; the system must project proposed grasp regions into metric Cartesian space using calibrated depth sensing and forward kinematics. Furthermore, environmental challenges such as specular reflections, dynamic shadows, and transient occlusions inevitably induce perceptual errors. Whatever algorithmic sophistication a proposer introduces, its execution demands must conform to the throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal dissipation envelope of the onboard processor.

A first estimate shows why one model cannot do both jobs. If every fresh evaluation must stream all of a model's weights from off-chip memory, its renewal rate can be no higher than the sustained bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights, a ceiling that falls in proportion to parameter count (@fig-cadence-gap). The intent model stores its weights as 4-bit integers (INT4, priced in @sec-brain-quantization) rather than 16-bit floating point (FP16), which raises its ceiling fourfold. Both of the machine's proposers still sit below their ceilings, because reading the input tokens in one pass through the model (the *prefill*) and then decoding the output add work that weight streaming alone ignores, and neither approaches the kilohertz rate at which the permission path and the servo loops run. The design problem is therefore deciding which computation can finish before the observation it started from goes stale. @Sec-brain-memory-wall derives the ceiling and the work above it; the figure is a preview of where the derivation lands.

::: {#fig-cadence-gap fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Cadence regimes on the machine's processor**: The weight-streaming ceiling $f \le \SustainedMemoryBandwidth/\WeightMemoryWeights$ on the mobile manipulator's application processor for FP16 and INT4 weights (16-bit floating-point and 4-bit integer representations, @sec-brain-quantization) plotted against model parameter counts, alongside the operating points for the machine's intent model and chunk policy. This ceiling establishes an upper bound on throughput rather than an achieved operating frequency, because input token prefill, vision encoding, and autoregressive generation consume execution cycles beyond raw DRAM weight traffic (@sec-brain-memory-wall)." fig-alt="Log-log plot of update rate against parameter count. Two parallel descending lines show the FP16 and INT4 weight-streaming ceilings. The chunk policy at 80 million parameters and 20 hertz and the intent model at 7 billion parameters and 2 hertz both sit below their ceilings. Shaded bands mark the permission-loop, chunk, and intent rate ranges."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-cadence-gap
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CADENCE REGIMES ON THE MACHINE'S PROCESSOR (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-cadence-gap, previewing @sec-brain-memory-wall
# │ Goal:    replace anonymous illustrative points with the computed
# │          weight-streaming ceiling and the machine's two proposers
# │ Show:    f_max = B_sustained / M_weights for FP16 and INT4 weights; intent
# │          model (7B, 2 Hz) and ACT chunk policy (80M, 20 Hz) below them
# │ How:     registry bandwidth x dram_efficiency; RM.intent_rate, RM.chunk_rate
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz, Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import GB, second, hertz, param, byte
from mlsysim.fmt import check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
_b_sus = (RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth * RM.dram_efficiency).to(GB / second).magnitude  # derived
_bpp = {"FP16 weights": 2.0, "INT4 weights": RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param.to(byte / param).magnitude}  # chosen
_intent = (RM.intent_model.parameters.to(param).magnitude, RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude)
_chunk = (RM.chunk_model.parameters.to(param).magnitude, RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
_n = np.logspace(7, 10.5, 200)
_ceiling = {k: _b_sus * 1e9 / (_n * v) for k, v in _bpp.items()}
_intent_wall = _b_sus * 1e9 / (_intent[0] * _bpp["INT4 weights"])
_chunk_wall = _b_sus * 1e9 / (_chunk[0] * 2.0)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(_intent[1] < _intent_wall, "Intent rate must sit below its INT4 streaming ceiling")
check(_chunk[1] < _chunk_wall, "Chunk rate must sit below its FP16 streaming ceiling")

# ┌── 5. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.axhspan(100, 1000, color="gray", alpha=0.12, label="Permission and servo loops (100–1000 Hz)")
# Vol IV roles: learned proposers in the proposal role (bronze); red is reserved for consequence.
PROPOSAL = "#B87333"
ax.axhspan(10, 50, color="#007A87", alpha=0.08, label="Chunk renewal (10–50 Hz)")
ax.axhspan(1, 5, color="#B87333", alpha=0.08, label="Intent revision (1–5 Hz)")
for (k, f), ls in zip(_ceiling.items(), ["-", "--"]):
    ax.plot(_n, f, ls, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=1.4, label=f"Streaming ceiling, {k}")
ax.plot(*_chunk, "o", ms=9, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "Chunk policy\n(ACT, 20 Hz)",
    xy=_chunk,
    xytext=(_chunk[0] * 0.18, _chunk[1] * 0.25),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PROPOSAL,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),
)
ax.plot(*_intent, "o", ms=9, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    "Intent model\n(INT4, 2 Hz)",
    xy=_intent,
    xytext=(_intent[0] * 0.05, _intent[1] * 0.3),
    fontsize=8,
    color=PROPOSAL,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),
)
ax.set_xlim(1e7, 3e10)
ax.set_ylim(0.3, 3e4)
ax.set_xlabel("Parameter count (log scale)")
ax.set_ylabel("Update rate [Hz] (log scale)")
plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

:::

Testing the two-speed design takes four steps. Classical pipelines built on hand-authored geometry and rigid state machines show why a learned proposer is needed at all, because open-world variability exhausts manual rule sets (@sec-brain-classical-wall). Learned representations restore semantic breadth but pay for it in tokens, cache, and bus traffic (@sec-brain-learned-representations). Pricing one fresh evaluation of the intent model on the application processor then exposes the memory wall and what quantization can and cannot do about it (@sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline), and sizing the chunks that keep the arm supplied separates the motion a chunk supplies from the time its evidence stays true (@sec-brain-chunk-supply). Because a proposal can arrive on schedule and still be wrong, the last step examines the failures that leave the permission path to refuse an on-time proposal (@sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities).

## The Classical Wall {#sec-brain-classical-wall}

In a fixed industrial workcell, a robotic gripper can approach the exact same fixture along an identical trajectory on every production cycle. Engineers can specify such repetitive motions through analytical geometry, rigid-body equations of motion, and deterministic state transitions. Classical control theory and traditional robotics flourish within this analytical formulation [@wiener1948cybernetics; @kalman1960new; @craig2005introduction]. The engineering challenge sharpens, however, when moving from a rigid fixture to an unconstrained scenario, such as retrieving a randomly oriented mug from a moving conveyor belt, where the engineer cannot enumerate every combination of object geometry, pose, and physical contact in advance.

Analytical kinematics and dynamics map target end-effector[^fn-endeffector-pose-kinematics] trajectories into joint angles, velocities, and actuator torques.[^fn-manipulator-dynamics-equation] Classical perception routines register incoming sensor point clouds against reference computer-aided design (CAD) models, while a synchronous finite-state machine steps the manipulator through sequential phases: approaching, aligning, grasping, and retracting. In a calibrated workcell, these analytical components reliably solve bounded manipulation tasks under explicit operational assumptions. Their computational latency and real-time execution bounds depend strictly on the chosen numerical solver, processor throughput, and contact dynamics model.

[^fn-endeffector-pose-kinematics]: **End-Effector**\index{End-effector!definition}: The tool, gripper, or hand at the distal tip of a manipulator, the only part of the arm meant to touch the workpiece. Workspace and keep-out checks are written against its pose rather than against joint angles, which is why the proposal payload later in this chapter carries end-effector poses alongside joint targets.

[^fn-manipulator-dynamics-equation]: **Manipulator Equation**\index{Rigid-body dynamics!manipulator equation}\index{Equations of motion!manipulator dynamics}: Classical control computes joint torques from $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \GravitationalTorqueVector = \boldsymbol{\tau}$, with a configuration-dependent inertia matrix $\ArticulatedInertiaMatrix$, Coriolis and centripetal terms $\CoriolisMatrix$, and gravity $\mathbf{g}$. Torque is linear in inertia, and a link's inertia grows with the square of its distance from the joint, so an outstretched arm needs more torque for the same angular acceleration. Unmodeled contact, friction, or deformable objects break this rigid-body model, which is the gap learned proposers enter; @sec-appendix-control-feedback-lin shows how classical control inverts this model to compute torque.

Where the operational environment remains structured and bounded, classical methods provide dependable behavior within their modeled operating envelopes. In a body shop (@fig-industrial-welding), the chassis sits in submillimeter tooling fixtures, the lighting never changes, and interlock fencing keeps people out of the cell during live cycles, so every quantity the controller depends on is fixed by construction. Within the causal boundary, this controlled regime permits explicit physical modeling, deterministic servo timing, and formal Lyapunov stability analysis.[^fn-lyapunov-stability-certificate] Control engineers can analytically guarantee trajectory tracking error bounds ($\lVert \mathbf{e}(t) \rVert \le \epsilon$) and certify software execution against rigorous functional safety standards without collecting empirical training datasets.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The causal boundary, where an admitted command becomes physical work, is established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.
:::

::: {#fig-industrial-welding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Industrial spot-welding workcell**: Multiple six-degree-of-freedom articulated robots execute preprogrammed spot welding paths on stamped automotive chassis at the BMW Leipzig plant. Operating in a calibrated factory environment with submillimeter repeatable fixtures and safety interlock cages, classical controllers provide deterministic cycle timing and formal stability proofs. (Credit: BMW Werk Leipzig, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:BMW_Leipzig_MEDIA_050719_Download_Karosseriebau_max.jpg), CC BY-SA 2.0 DE.)" fig-alt="Articulated industrial robots executing automated spot welding on an automotive chassis within a safety-caged factory cell."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_industrial_welding.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

[^fn-lyapunov-stability-certificate]: **Lyapunov Stability**\index{Lyapunov stability!energy-like certificate}: Aleksandr Lyapunov's 1892 method proves that a system returns to equilibrium by exhibiting an energy-like function that decreases along every trajectory, without solving the equations of motion [@slotine1991applied]. Writing that function down requires an explicit dynamics model, which is why the method certifies a classical controller and not a learned proposer. The barrier certificates of @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission reuse the idea to keep the machine inside a safe set rather than at a point.

Yet when an embodied machine steps outside the structured factory cage into unstructured, open-world environments, this analytical paradigm hits the **classical wall** [@brooks1991intelligence; @levine2018learning]. Physical reality defies closed-form geometric modeling: real objects deform under contact, ambient illumination shifts unpredictably, and scenes exhibit near-infinite visual and mechanical variety. A rescue test arena of tilted ramps and a victim dummy on a high shelf (@fig-unstructured-rescue) has none of the fixtures that made the welding cell analyzable: no part arrives at a known pose, and no template describes the terrain. In such unmapped, irregular settings, preauthored geometric templates and rigid state machines lose state coverage and fail to generalize.

::: {#fig-unstructured-rescue fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Unstructured search-and-rescue robot**: A four-wheeled rescue robot carrying cameras and a laser scanner on a pan-tilt mast works through a test arena of tilted ramps and narrow openings, with a victim dummy placed on a high shelf. In such unmapped environments, preauthored geometric models and rigid state machines can lose coverage; learned policies may help infer spatial affordances and traversability from sensory streams. (Credit: Hector, Technische Universität Darmstadt, at the 2010 RoboCup German Open; photo by Mike1024, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:RoboCup_Rescue_robot_Hector_from_Darmstadt_at_2010_German_open.jpg), public domain.)" fig-alt="Four-wheeled robot with a sensor mast on tilted plywood ramps in a rescue test arena, seen through a round cutout, with a doll on a shelf in the background."}
![](images/jpg/fig03_real_unstructured_rescue.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Outside structured fixtures, the analytical perception-and-control pipeline fractures under perceptual uncertainty and environmental permutation. A rigid CAD template fails when handling deformable textiles or asymmetric food items; specular reflections or cast shadows can obliterate the depth discontinuities required to segment adjacent parcels; and an unexpected obstacle invalidates the guard conditions of a preauthored grasping state machine. While engineers can introduce additional templates, heuristic filtering thresholds, and recovery branches to patch edge cases, this manual expansion triggers combinatorial complexity. Each added heuristic demands costly bespoke tuning and revalidation, yet still fails to deliver robust coverage across open-world distributions.

Machine learning offers an architectural exit from this combinatorial trap. By training over diverse physical interactions and expert demonstrations, neural representations learn to extract generalized spatial affordances and behavioral policies directly from high-dimensional sensor streams, without a hand-crafted geometric model for every item encountered. Yet this data-driven policy does not replace the downstream analytical controller. Deterministic feedback loops remain essential for enforcing kinematic safety bounds and tracking proposed trajectories at high update rates. Instead, learning introduces a computationally intensive, non-deterministic proposal stage whose memory bandwidth, arithmetic throughput, and inference latency must interface cleanly with the underlying real-time controller.

## Learned Representations {#sec-brain-learned-representations}

When commanded to pick an unfamiliar ceramic mug from a conveyor, a learned model relates the text prompt to visual features of the handle and proposes a plausible grasp region without an exact CAD model. VLA models combine multi-camera imagery, natural-language instructions, and proprioceptive robot state to produce candidate actions [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. These systems descend from early embodied language models such as SayCan and PaLM-E, which emitted high-level semantic plans rather than low-level motor commands [@ahn2022saycan; @driess2023palme]. The operational value of a VLA stems from broad generalization across diverse objects and ambient environments acquired during large-scale pretraining, rather than formal guarantees of correct scene interpretation.

Teleoperated demonstrations can likewise teach coordinated sensorimotor policies for tasks whose contacts and structural deformations resist analytic kinematic modeling. In a bimanual teleoperation workcell (@fig-aloha-manipulator), an operator moves low-cost leader arms while follower arms with parallel grippers reproduce the motion, and overhead and wrist cameras record what the followers saw; those recordings become the training data for policies that later act alone [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The running machine's chunk policy takes its size from ACT, which was trained on exactly such recordings, and what such a policy learns from them is the action chunk itself, a short stretch of the operator's motion predicted from one view. How demonstrations become a policy belongs to @sec-training; this chapter prices what the trained policy costs to run. Although learned representations tolerate sensory variations captured across training distributions, executing any proposed motion safely still demands calibrated spatial geometry and strict physical boundary enforcement. Empirical task success demonstrates capability over tested operating envelopes, but out-of-distribution shifts in illumination, surface friction, or payload dynamics can quickly induce behavioral drift or outright failure.

The computational cost of this capability depends directly on the model's underlying representation. A transformer does not read pixels or words directly; it reads *tokens*\index{Token!embedding of an input slice}, embedding vectors that each represent one slice of input, such as an image patch, a word fragment, or a joint angle. @Fig-vla-architecture traces that token dataflow from camera patches through self-attention to candidate action chunks. Multi-view camera frames consume significant memory bandwidth during ingestion, historical context expands key-value (KV) cache footprints in memory, and the inference engine must produce subsequent actions before the physical state diverges from the initial observation. Evaluating an embodied learned model alongside a classical perception-planning pipeline requires assessing both task generalization and the end-to-end latency required to refresh action proposals.

::: {#fig-aloha-manipulator fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Bimanual teleoperation workcell**: Dual-arm teleoperation setup featuring two six-degree-of-freedom follower arms, two leader arms for kinesthetic teleoperation, multi-view cameras (overhead and wrist-mounted), and parallel grippers mounted to an extruded aluminum frame. The physical AI policy ingests synchronized multi-camera streams to predict continuous end-effector trajectories, and the permission path must refuse any proposal that would cause self-collision or motor over-torquing during closed-loop execution. (Credit: ALOHA 2 Team, ALOHA 2: An Enhanced Low-Cost Hardware for Bimanual Teleoperation, arXiv:2405.02292, CC BY 4.0.)" fig-alt="Dual-arm robotic teleoperation workstation with leader and follower arms, overhead cameras, and grippers mounted on an aluminum frame."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_aloha_manipulator.png){width="85%"}
:::

::: {#fig-vla-architecture fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Embodied Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture**: A representative dataflow. (1) Camera patches receive 2D image-position and camera identifiers alongside language and robot-state tokens; metric depth still requires calibrated evidence. (2) Self-attention mixes the combined token sequence; the colored grid illustrates internal attention weights, not a verified affordance or grasp pose. (3) Autoregressive token decoders emit tokens sequentially, whereas one-pass chunk heads and iterative action experts generate candidate multi-step chunks ($\ActionChunk_{t:t+\Horizon-1}$) in one pass or over several refinement steps. (4) An independent permission path checks candidate motion against sensed state and modeled limits before actuation. (Synthesized from Brohan et al. [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2], Kim et al. [@kim2024openvla], and Octo Model Team [@octo_2023])." fig-alt="Comprehensive architectural schematic of a Vision-Language-Action foundation model showing spatial patch slicing, 2D positional embeddings, multimodal self-attention weights in an illustrative image grid, discrete vs. continuous action decoders, and an independent proposal boundary."}

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PUBLISHED VLA AND DUAL-SYSTEM FIGURES (STATE OF PRACTICE, AS OF 2026)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: item 3 of @sec-brain-learned-representations, the decoder-family
# │          paragraphs of @sec-brain-action-chunking, @tbl-03-state-of-practice
# │ Goal:    hold every published 2023-2025 system figure the chapter quotes in
# │          one place, each with its source, so the dated table can be refreshed
# │          without touching the argument
# │ Show:    horizons (DP 16/8, pi0 50, ACT 100); OFT 26x; FAST 30-60 tokens;
# │          Helix, GR00T N1, Gemini Robotics rates
# │ How:     literature values, each verified against the paper on 2026-09-29;
# │          promotion candidates for mlsysim literature/registry
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_params, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_memory, check

class StateOfPractice:
    """Published architecture figures, verified against each source (2026-09-29)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # Chi et al. 2024 (Diffusion Policy): prediction horizon T_p and executed T_a
    dp_predict, dp_execute = 16, 8  # category: literature
    # Zhao et al. 2023 (ACT): chunk size k = 100 at 50 Hz
    act_k = 100  # category: literature
    act_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (ACT control rate)
    # Black et al. 2024 (pi0), Sec. IV and App. A-D
    pi0_params = 3.3e9 * param  # category: literature (total)
    pi0_expert = 300e6 * param  # category: literature (action expert)
    pi0_h = 50  # category: literature
    pi0_steps = 10  # category: literature (flow integration steps)
    pi0_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature ("up to 50 Hz")
    pi0_latency = 73 * millisecond  # category: literature (on-board, RTX 4090)
    # Kim et al. 2024 (OpenVLA): about 6 Hz on one RTX 4090 in bfloat16
    openvla_rate = 6 * hertz  # category: literature
    # Kim, Finn, Liang 2025 (OpenVLA-OFT): LIBERO, A100, 8-step chunks
    oft_hz, openvla_hz_a100, oft_chunk = 109.7 * hertz, 4.2 * hertz, 8  # category: literature
    # Pertsch et al. 2025 (FAST): 30-60 tokens per chunk; pi0-FAST ~750 ms vs pi0 ~100 ms (RTX 4090)
    fast_tok_lo, fast_tok_hi = 30, 60  # category: literature
    fast_naive, fast_tok_50hz = 700, 53  # category: literature (shirt fold, 50 Hz, Table I)
    fast_task_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (shirt-fold control rate, Table I)
    fast_latency, flow_latency = 750 * millisecond, 100 * millisecond  # category: literature (approximate)
    # Figure AI 2025 (Helix)
    helix_s2_params, helix_s1_params = 7e9 * param, 80e6 * param  # category: literature
    helix_s2_lo, helix_s2_hi, helix_s1_rate = 7 * hertz, 9 * hertz, 200 * hertz  # category: literature
    helix_dof = 35  # category: literature
    # Bjorck et al. 2025 (GR00T N1)
    gr00t_params, gr00t_vlm = 2.2e9 * param, 1.34e9 * param  # category: literature
    gr00t_s2_rate, gr00t_s1_rate = 10 * hertz, 120 * hertz  # category: literature
    gr00t_h, gr00t_steps = 16, 4  # category: literature
    gr00t_latency = 63.9 * millisecond  # category: literature (16-action chunk, L40, bf16)
    # Gemini Robotics Team 2025 (Gemini Robotics): cloud backbone plus on-robot decoder
    gemini_backbone = 160 * millisecond  # category: literature (upper bound, "under 160 ms")
    gemini_e2e = 250 * millisecond  # category: literature ("approximately 250 ms")
    gemini_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature (effective control rate with chunks)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    oft_speedup = (oft_hz / openvla_hz_a100).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    fast_ratio = fast_naive / fast_tok_50hz

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(oft_speedup - 26.1) < 0.05, f"OFT speedup drifted: {oft_speedup}")
    check(abs(fast_ratio - 13.2) < 0.05, f"FAST compression drifted: {fast_ratio}")
    check(dp_execute < dp_predict < pi0_h < act_k, "Horizon ordering drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    dp_predict_str, dp_execute_str, act_k_str = fmt_int(dp_predict), fmt_int(dp_execute), fmt_int(act_k)
    act_rate_str = fmt_frequency(act_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    pi0_params_str = fmt_params(pi0_params, precision=1)
    pi0_expert_str = fmt_params(pi0_expert, precision=0)
    pi0_h_str, pi0_steps_str = fmt_int(pi0_h), fmt_int(pi0_steps)
    pi0_rate_str = fmt_frequency(pi0_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    pi0_latency_str = fmt_latency(pi0_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    openvla_rate_str = fmt_frequency(openvla_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    oft_hz_str = fmt_frequency(oft_hz, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    openvla_hz_a100_str = fmt_frequency(openvla_hz_a100, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    oft_chunk_str = fmt_int(oft_chunk)
    oft_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(oft_speedup), precision=0)  # the paper reports "26x"
    fast_tok_lo_str, fast_tok_hi_str = fmt_int(fast_tok_lo), fmt_int(fast_tok_hi)
    fast_naive_str, fast_tok_50hz_str = fmt_int(fast_naive), fmt_int(fast_tok_50hz)
    fast_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(fast_ratio, precision=1)
    fast_task_rate_str = fmt_frequency(fast_task_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    fast_latency_str = fmt_latency(fast_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    flow_latency_str = fmt_latency(flow_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    helix_s2_params_str = fmt_params(helix_s2_params, precision=0)
    helix_s1_params_str = fmt_params(helix_s1_params, precision=0)
    helix_s2_lo_num_str = fmt_int(helix_s2_lo.magnitude)

    helix_s1_rate_str = fmt_frequency(helix_s1_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-token-footprint
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TOKEN AND CACHE FOOTPRINT OF THE ILLUSTRATIVE THREE-CAMERA BACKBONE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: items 1-2 of the dataflow list in @sec-brain-learned-representations
# │ Goal:    replace the hand-typed patch, token, embedding, and KV-cache values
# │          with values read from the intent model's registered shape
# │ Show:    (224/14)^2 = 256 patches; 3 x 256 = 768 visual tokens; S ~ 800;
# │          800 x 4096 x 2 bytes ~ 6.55 MB embedding; 2 x 32 x 4096 x 2 =
# │          524,288 bytes (~0.524 MB) of KV cache per token
# │ How:     RM.intent_model.layers and .hidden_dim; the camera count, frame
# │          size, patch size, and prompt/state token counts are illustrative
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import byte, MB
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_display_math, check

class TokenFootprint:
    """Patch, token, embedding, and per-token KV sizes for the illustrative backbone."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator.intent_model  # category: chosen
    n_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    d_model = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    cameras = 3  # category: illustrative (left wrist, right wrist, overhead)
    frame_px = 224  # category: illustrative (square input frame)
    patch_px = 14  # category: illustrative (ViT patch size)
    prompt_tokens = 32  # category: illustrative
    state_tokens = 16  # category: illustrative
    s_round = 800  # category: illustrative (rounded context length)
    elem_bytes = 2  # category: chosen (FP16)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    patches = (frame_px // patch_px) ** 2
    visual_tokens = cameras * patches
    embed_mem = (s_round * d_model * elem_bytes * byte).to(MB)
    kv_token_bytes = 2 * n_layers * d_model * elem_bytes
    kv_token_mem = (kv_token_bytes * byte).to(MB)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(patches == 256 and visual_tokens == 768, f"Patch count drifted: {patches}, {visual_tokens}")
    check(visual_tokens + prompt_tokens + state_tokens > s_round, "S must exceed the rounded 800 tokens")
    check(n_layers == 32 and d_model == 4096, f"Backbone shape drifted: {n_layers} x {d_model}")
    check(kv_token_bytes == 524288, f"KV bytes per token drifted: {kv_token_bytes}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    cameras_str = fmt_int(cameras)
    patches_str = fmt_int(patches)
    visual_tokens_str = fmt_int(visual_tokens)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_int(prompt_tokens)
    state_tokens_str = fmt_int(state_tokens)
    s_round_str = fmt_int(s_round)
    n_layers_str = fmt_int(n_layers)
    d_model_str = fmt_int(d_model, commas=False)
    kv_token_bytes_str = fmt_int(kv_token_bytes)
    kv_token_mb_str = fmt_memory(kv_token_mem, unit=MB, precision=3)
    embed_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{embed}}}} = S \times d \times 2\,\text{{bytes}} = {s_round} \times {d_model} \times 2 \approx {embed_mem.magnitude:.2f}\,\text{{MB}}"
    )
```

To grasp the mug, the model turns camera images and a language instruction into candidate trajectories in three learned stages: tokenization, attention across the tokens in a backbone, and an action decoder that projects the backbone's output into proposed motion. A proposal boundary separates all three from actuation, so every candidate action passes independent permission checks before it reaches the motor drives. Evaluating this pipeline from a systems perspective means tracing what each stage stores in memory, transfers across the memory bus, and delivers to the controllers below it:

1. *Sensory ingestion and spatial tokenization (the inputs).*
   A vision transformer (ViT) frontend [@dosovitskiy2020image] slices each incoming camera frame into a grid of non-overlapping pixel patches of size $p_{\text{patch}}{\times}p_{\text{patch}}$ (typically $14{\times}14$ or $16{\times}16$ pixels). Each patch is linearly projected into a vector of width $\HiddenDimension$, augmented with a position embedding (learned in the SigLIP and DINOv2 encoders that OpenVLA uses [@kim2024openvla], sinusoidal in some other designs), and tagged with a learned camera identifier.

   In an illustrative three-camera configuration (left wrist, right wrist, and an overhead torso mount) capturing $224{\times}224$ images, the image frontend prepares a buffer for each view. Each frame yields $(224 / 14)^2 =$ `{python} TokenFootprint.patches_str` spatial patches. Across `{python} TokenFootprint.cameras_str` cameras, ingestion injects `{python} TokenFootprint.visual_tokens_str` visual tokens into the model's sequence on every perceptual step. When concatenated with tokenized natural language commands (about `{python} TokenFootprint.prompt_tokens_str` tokens) and proprioceptive joint state embeddings (about `{python} TokenFootprint.state_tokens_str` tokens), the initial context runs slightly past `{python} TokenFootprint.s_round_str` tokens, which the estimates below round to $\SequenceLength \approx$ `{python} TokenFootprint.s_round_str`. In 16-bit floating-point (FP16) precision ($2\,\text{bytes}$ per element) with hidden dimension $\HiddenDimension =$ `{python} TokenFootprint.d_model_str`, the token embeddings for one such step occupy
   `{python} TokenFootprint.embed_display_math`
   a few megabytes, negligible beside the multi-gigabyte weights that @sec-brain-memory-wall prices. Tokens therefore cost the machine through the arithmetic every weight performs on each of them and through the cache they leave behind, not through the storage of the embeddings themselves. Neither 2D image coordinates nor internal attention patterns constitute metric depth. Projecting an end-effector into physical 3D space requires calibrated extrinsic camera matrices and depth telemetry.

2. *Multimodal alignment and attention (the backbone).*
   For the illustrative backbone, the token sequence passes through $\NumberOfLayers =$ `{python} TokenFootprint.n_layers_str` transformer layers where standard multi-head self-attention computes pairwise token interactions [@vaswani2017attention]. To relate each new token to the earlier ones, every layer keeps a *key* and a *value* vector for every token it has already processed, the **KV cache**\index{KV cache!definition}. The arithmetic of attention grows with the square of the sequence length ($\mathcal{O}(\SequenceLength^2 \HiddenDimension)$ FLOPs), but the memory the cache occupies grows only linearly with it, as @eq-brain-kv-cache gives:
   $$\KvcacheMemory = 2 \times \NumberOfLayers \times \HiddenDimension \times \SequenceLength \times \ElementStorageSize$$ {#eq-brain-kv-cache}
   The estimate assumes full-width keys and values, meaning every attention head in every layer stores its own. For a `{python} TokenFootprint.n_layers_str`-layer model with $\HiddenDimension =$ `{python} TokenFootprint.d_model_str` using FP16 storage, each context token then claims `{python} TokenFootprint.kv_token_bytes_str` bytes, about `{python} TokenFootprint.kv_token_mb_str`, of KV cache, so an observation step of several hundred tokens holds hundreds of megabytes.

   Whether the machine pays that charge more than once depends on what the model keeps between evaluations. Single-observation VLAs such as OpenVLA rebuild their context from each new frame and carry no cache across control steps, and the running machine's intent model is one of them. Only a design that conditions on retained history rereads the cache on every step, and @sec-brain-two-proposers prices what retaining several seconds of history would cost. Such rereading is not free, because the processor uses a unified memory architecture (UMA), in which the CPU, the GPU, and the camera interfaces share one DRAM. Every byte of cache read is bus time taken from weight streaming and from the direct memory access (DMA) transfers that deliver sensor frames. Grouped-query attention (GQA) narrows the cache by letting several query heads share one key and value; cross-attention can instead limit which retained representations the decoder reads. Either saving depends on the architecture, and action chunking does not provide it.

   Attention weights are also not geometry. A strong weight between the language tokens "mug handle" and a visual patch does not establish a graspable affordance[^fn-affordance-grasp-planning] or collision-free clearance, and the KV cache does not keep track of an object while it is occluded. The formal patch-embedding, position-encoding, and attention formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-patch-embedding.

3. *Specialized action decoders (the outputs).*
   Instead of generating open-ended conversational text, the final hidden representation $\mathbf{h}_{\text{context}} \in \mathbb{R}^\HiddenDimension$ is routed to specialized action decoders. The running machine's chunk policy proposes base velocity and arm targets together in one whole-body stream (@sec-brain-two-proposers), so its decoder is a manipulation decoder whose outputs include the base; separate navigation models that decode waypoints over a topological map of the building (@fig-vln-navigation) follow the same proposal rules but are not part of this machine. Manipulation (VLA) models diverge sharply in how they bridge semantic representations to physical motion:

   Discrete action decoders map each action dimension to a categorical token by dividing its continuous range into bins [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. Autoregressive decoders such as RT-2 and OpenVLA then generate those tokens sequentially, requiring one complete model evaluation per action dimension [@brohan2023rt2; @kim2024openvla]. However, discretization does not fundamentally mandate sequential decoding. RT-1 predicts all action tokens simultaneously in a single forward pass, and its authors demonstrated that autoregressively conditioning each action dimension on preceding dimensions yielded no accuracy gains while more than doubling inference latency [@brohan2023rt1].

   What separates modern decoders in systems practice is the computational cost of generating a trajectory chunk and the volume of model weights reread during inference. Three architectural families dominate implementations as of 2026:

   * *Autoregressive tokens.* Each token requires a separate sequential evaluation. With one token per action dimension per control step, predicting a chunk of $\Horizon$ timesteps across $\ActionDimension$ dimensions demands $\Horizon \ActionDimension$ sequential evaluations, causing inference latency to scale with both horizon and degree of freedom. Per-step binning also breaks down at high control frequencies: consecutive continuous setpoints differ negligibly, producing runs of identical token targets from which next-token training learns almost nothing. Frequency-space action sequence tokenization (FAST) resolves this scaling bottleneck by applying a discrete cosine transform across each action dimension over the chunk horizon, representing the trajectory as a linear combination of cosine basis functions [@pertsch2025fast]. Smooth physical motions concentrate energy in low-frequency coefficients, allowing aggressive truncation. FAST quantizes these coefficients and compresses them with byte-pair encoding, which repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols into a new token, tying token counts directly to trajectory information complexity rather than $\Horizon \ActionDimension$. On a `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_task_rate_str` bimanual task, FAST compressed `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_naive_str` raw binned tokens to `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_tok_50hz_str`, achieving a `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_ratio_mult_str` reduction [@pertsch2025fast]. Nevertheless, token generation remains sequential: the authors report an inference latency of approximately `{python} StateOfPractice.fast_latency_str` per chunk for FAST-$\pi_0$, compared to `{python} StateOfPractice.flow_latency_str` for the flow-matching variant on an identical desktop GPU.
   * *One-pass chunk heads.* Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) regresses an entire trajectory chunk in a single feedforward decoder pass [@zhao2023learning]. OpenVLA-OFT adapts an autoregressive VLA into a one-pass generator by passing placeholder action tokens through bidirectional self-attention and directly regressing continuous values for all action steps in parallel, increasing throughput by `{python} StateOfPractice.oft_speedup_mult_str` on `{python} StateOfPractice.oft_chunk_str`-step chunks [@kim2025openvlaoft]. However, deterministic regression heads trained with mean squared error struggle with multimodal demonstration data: when presented with two equally valid paths around an obstacle, a naive regression loss averages them into an infeasible trajectory directly through the obstacle [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. ACT mitigates this failure mode by conditioning its decoder on a latent style variable, a code that records which of several demonstrated ways of doing the task a trajectory follows, learned with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE, @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal).
   * *Iterative action experts.* Diffusion Policy formulates action generation as iterative denoising, starting a candidate chunk from random noise and repeatedly removing the noise a network predicts, adapting continuous diffusion processes originally developed for generative vision models [@ho2020denoising; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. The $\pi_0$ architecture pairs a `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_expert_str`-parameter flow-matching[^fn-flow-matching-steps] **action expert**\index{Action expert!flow matching} with a pretrained vision-language model, yielding `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_params_str` total parameters [@black2024pi0]. The large vision-language backbone processes perceptual observations once and caches its key-value activations; the action expert then generates the continuous trajectory chunk across `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_steps_str` numerical integration steps while attending to that static cache. Each integration step is a forward Euler step. The expert starts the candidate from Gaussian noise, evaluates a learned velocity field that says which direction moves it toward a plausible action chunk, and moves the candidate a small distance that way; after `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_steps_str` steps the candidate is the chunk. Each step requires a forward pass only through the lightweight action expert and its cross-attention reads into the cached backbone KV activations, avoiding any re-evaluation of the multi-billion-parameter vision-language backbone. Subsequent designs such as $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1 employ this exact decoupling [@black2025pi05; @bjorck2025gr00t], with $\pi_{0.5}$ combining FAST-token pretraining on the backbone with flow-expert execution at runtime.

   Across all three families, the continuous output forms a multi-step trajectory chunk:
   $$\ActionChunk_{t:t+\Horizon-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \mathbf{a}_{t+1}, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+\Horizon-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{\Horizon \times \ActionDimension}$$
   Here $\Horizon$ specifies the future prediction horizon in discrete setpoints and $\ActionDimension$ denotes the degrees of freedom per action; @sec-brain-action-chunking states the formal definition (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) once the memory wall has shown why chunks are needed. Published horizons span from tens to hundreds of setpoints: Diffusion Policy predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.dp_predict_str` steps and executes the initial `{python} StateOfPractice.dp_execute_str` [@chi2024diffusionpolicy], $\pi_0$ predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_h_str` steps [@black2024pi0], and ACT predicts `{python} StateOfPractice.act_k_str` steps at `{python} StateOfPractice.act_rate_str` [@zhao2023learning]. The structural gap between prediction and execution horizons resurfaces in @sec-brain-two-proposers as the interface between asynchronous trajectory generation and real-time permission filtering. A trajectory chunk provides an open-loop sequence of future setpoints derived from a single sensory context, amortizing inference latency without incorporating intervening sensor observations. @Sec-brain-action-chunking evaluates the computational efficiency of these three decoder families on target silicon, while @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal gives the discrete tokenization rule and details how generative decoders capture multimodal demonstration distributions without averaging conflicting trajectories.

4. *The proposal boundary (isolation from actuators).*
   Whether the model plans navigation or manipulation, its output constitutes an unprivileged candidate proposal situated strictly outside the proposal boundary (definition \ref{dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary}).\index{Unprivileged proposal!proposal boundary} Under the concrete machine model established in @sec-boundary-machine-model, the foundation model executes within unprivileged user space on the host application processor and possesses no direct memory-mapped access to pulse-width modulation (PWM) registers or motor coil current drivers.

   The Brain transfers candidate motion proposals alongside the timestamps of the sensory frames that generated them. Downstream real-time loops operating at kilohertz frequencies track admitted trajectory setpoints and regulate motor current using closed-loop encoder and torque telemetry. Protracted neural inference delays cannot preempt or suspend these low-latency control loops, nor can an unverified model proposal bypass safety invariants. @Sec-brain-memory-wall analyzes the DRAM bandwidth limits of refreshing these evaluations.

   Candidate proposals reach the permission path through an explicit architectural handoff. This permission layer rejects unsafe or physically ungrounded proposals whenever telemetry indicates impending collisions, joint limit violations, or kinematic singularities (arm configurations in which the joints lose the ability to move the end effector in some direction), immediately engaging a deterministic fallback controller. @Sec-nervous-actuation-authority isolates this gating logic on a dedicated real-time safety microcontroller, completely segregated from the application processor hosting the learned model.

[^fn-affordance-grasp-planning]: **Affordance**: Gibson's term for the action possibilities an environment offers an agent, defined jointly by object properties and agent physical capabilities [@gibson1979ecological]. A handle affords a grasp only when its physical dimensions and clearance accommodate the robot's gripper geometry and kinematics. While self-attention weights across image patches highlight semantically relevant features such as a handle, they do not certify mechanical grasp stability or kinematic reachability, the failure mode @sec-brain-semantic-hallucinations analyzes. \index{Affordances!grasp geometry}

[^fn-flow-matching-steps]: **Flow Matching**: A training framework that trains a neural network to model a continuous velocity field transporting probability density from Gaussian noise to empirical data distributions along straight trajectories [@lipman2022flow]. These rectified probability paths allow numerical solvers to generate high-fidelity samples in relatively few integration steps, whereas conventional denoising diffusion models often required hundreds or thousands of sequential iterations [@ho2020denoising]. In an embedded robotics architecture, this integration step count represents a direct hardware latency bottleneck, as each solver step rereads the action expert's weight parameters and accesses the cached visual context from off-chip memory. \index{Flow matching!integration steps}

::: {#fig-vln-navigation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Topological vision-language navigation**: Embodied navigation architecture executing natural-language spatial instructions. Panoramic visual observations are encoded into perceptual tokens, matched against prompt embeddings, and cross-referenced with a dynamically updated topological navigation graph. The action decoder prunes unreachable nodes and emits metric waypoint offsets $(\Delta x, \Delta y)$ and heading setpoints to guide the chassis along traversable semantic frontiers without requiring an exact geometric prior map. (Adapted from @an2023etpnav, arXiv:2304.03047, CC BY 4.0.)" fig-alt="Schematic of topological vision-language navigation showing panoramic observation tokens, topological graph matching, and decoded waypoint offsets and heading setpoints."}
![](images/png/fig03_real_vln_topological_navigation.png){width="95%"}
:::

The choice of sensory representation and action decoder dictates the memory traffic and latency profile of every control cycle. Maintaining historical token context accumulates KV cache overhead that consumes memory bus bandwidth, while running multi-billion-parameter backbones on resource-constrained embedded systems demands massive weight streaming from off-chip DRAM. An embodied agent needs both semantic breadth and rapid trajectory renewal, and these costs suggest that one monolithic model on an embedded processor cannot deliver both. Whether it can is a question of numbers, and the place to get them is one fresh evaluation of the machine's intent model on its own application processor.

## The Cost of a Fresh Evaluation {#sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline}

At the pick station the mobile manipulator's arm consumes a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds, while the mug keeps moving along the conveyor. Whether one large model could supply those setpoints depends on how long one fresh evaluation of it takes on the application processor, and that time depends on which resource the evaluation exhausts first, the memory bus or the arithmetic units. This section prices that evaluation for the machine's intent model and asks what quantization can buy back; @sec-brain-chunk-supply then checks the motion buffer that the selected split relies on against the target's drift. The single large-model cases below are alternatives used to expose the trade-off, not changes to the selected machine.

After ingestion (the tokenization of @sec-brain-learned-representations), four learned stages turn those tokens into action proposals, and each hands the next a record that ages (@fig-cognitive-pipeline). Across the proposal boundary, an isolated safety microcontroller (MCU) running the permission path on a `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick decides whether candidate setpoints become admitted drive commands. These stages describe what the machine must compute, not how its networks are divided; the three learned stages of @sec-brain-learned-representations describe the inside of one transformer. On the running machine, the intent model recognizes the mug and names the target (perception and intent), a tracker carries the mug's estimate from frame to frame (memory), and the chunk policy, reading its own camera frames, turns the target into setpoints (planning). *Memory* here means the belief the machine keeps about the world, not DRAM. The chapters of Part III, beginning with @sec-perception, develop each stage in depth; here they matter only for what each hands downstream and how quickly that record goes stale.

Perception grounds what it recognizes in metric coordinates relative to the base, so that the mug has a 3D position and orientation (an $\SpecialEuclideanGroup$ pose)[^fn-se3-pose-group] and a graspable handle rather than an abstract semantic label; its output ages from the moment of capture. Memory carries those estimates through occlusion and must let each one expire when the evidence behind it does. Intent decomposes a task such as "take the ceramic mug off the conveyor and hand it to the coworker at the packing station" into subgoals, and because the mug moves while the intent model deliberates, it hands the planner a target that expires, an intent lease\index{Intent lease!temporal contract} in the vocabulary of Part III. Planning converts that target into candidate setpoints for the base and the arm, the proposals the permission path will judge.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The observation contract that dates each perception output from its capture epoch is developed in @sec-perception-observation-contract.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The intent lease and the deadlines that end it are developed in @sec-intent-lease.
:::

These stages, and the ingestion before them, all run on the application processor and draw on the same memory bus, which is where the machine's cadence is decided. Its memory bandwidth, arithmetic rate, and power envelope are fixed allocations, and scaling the model up only draws harder against them. The rest of this section measures what they cost the intent model.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ That every added layer of onboard compute draws against fixed memory bandwidth, electrical power, and thermal dissipation is established in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws.
:::

[^fn-se3-pose-group]: **SE(3) Pose**\index{Special Euclidean group!SE(3) grounding}\index{Metric spatial grounding}: SE(3), the special Euclidean group in three dimensions, is the set of rigid-body poses, a rotation plus a translation with six degrees of freedom; "special" excludes mirror reflections, which no rigid object can undergo. A pose can be compared with measured depth and aged from its capture time, while a semantic label such as "mug handle" can be neither, which is why the handoff to planning is a pose and not a label.

::: {#fig-cognitive-pipeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI cognitive flow**: The learned stages run on the application processor and each hands the next a record that ages: ingestion produces tokens, perception a metric pose with its age, memory a belief with its evidence epoch, intent an intent lease, and planning candidate setpoints. Everything up to planning is proposal. Only the permission path, on its own `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` tick across the proposal boundary, can turn a proposal into an admitted command for the drives." fig-alt="Two rows of boxes. Top row: sensors (cameras, IMU, encoders) feed ingestion (hands on tokens), which feeds perception (hands on pose plus age), which feeds memory (hands on belief plus epoch). An arrow wraps from memory down to the second row: intent (hands on intent lease) feeds planning (hands on candidate setpoints). The learned stages sit inside a dashed region labeled application processor. A dashed proposal arrow from planning crosses a vertical dashed line labeled proposal boundary into a permission path box (safety MCU, 1 kHz tick), which sends an admitted command to drives and plant."}
![](images/svg/fig03_cognitive_pipeline_horizontal.svg){width="100%"}
:::

On an edge robotics system-on-chip (SoC) with unified memory, model weights, sensor transfers, and host computation share memory bandwidth. A policy cannot budget the full bus for itself while assuming that new camera frames arrive without interference. The transfer bound below is therefore a lower bound on evaluation time; the worked comparison later uses an assumed sustained fraction of peak bandwidth. @Sec-placement-resource-contention models how weight fetches, camera transfers, and telemetry writes queue for the shared memory controller.

### The memory wall {#sec-brain-memory-wall}

When each evaluation streams weights that cannot remain on-chip, memory bandwidth can limit the update cadence of an embodied neural policy even when arithmetic capacity is available. The memory wall\index{Memory wall!physical inference} describes the limit imposed when operands cannot reach arithmetic units fast enough to use their available throughput. In physical AI, the consequence is a delayed proposal while the body continues moving.

On-chip static RAM (SRAM) and caches can reuse weights and intermediate state without another external transfer, but only while the working set fits the memory available to that workload. Off-chip low-power DRAM (LPDDR5) provides much greater capacity through a narrower shared interface. Cache sizes, access latency, and attainable bandwidth depend on the particular processor and allocation; nominal chip-wide capacity does not establish that an action head will remain resident.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-intent-model-latency
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INTENT-MODEL LATENCY: MEMORY WALL PLUS PREFILL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-intent-model-latency (canonical memory-wall example),
# │          @fig-patterson-roofline, and the two-proposer notebook
# │ Goal:    price one fresh intent-model evaluation from both roofline terms
# │          and show which rate the machine can state
# │ Show:    98.04 ms FP16 sweep (10.2 Hz wall); 188.5 ms compute-bound prefill
# │          of S = 288 tokens; 6 decode sweeps; FP16 total 777 ms; INT4 total
# │          336 ms (2.98 Hz) against the 336 ms Jetson measurement; 2 Hz rate
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency (prefill max(F/(u Pi), sweep) plus
# │          (D - 1) bandwidth-bound decode sweeps); RM.intent_latency_breakdown
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_qty,
    fmt_arithmetic_intensity,
    fmt_display_math,
    sci_latex,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class IntentModelLatency:
    """One fresh intent-model evaluation: FP16 memory wall, prefill, decode, INT4."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (OpenVLA-sized intent model)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    n_params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    n_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    d_model = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    d_action = model.action_dim  # category: datasheet (one token per action dimension)
    s_in = RM.intent_input_tokens  # category: illustrative (256 patches derived + 32 prompt)
    patches = 256  # category: derived; (224 / 14)^2 patches for one 224 x 224 view
    pi_fp16 = soc.compute.precision_flops["fp16"]  # category: datasheet (dense FP16 GPU)
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    eta = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative (sustained fraction of peak)
    u = RM.intent_compute_utilization  # category: illustrative (achieved fraction of FP16 peak)
    bpp_fp16 = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (FP16 weights)
    bpp_int4 = RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param  # category: chosen (INT4 weights, deployed)
    t_measured = RM.intent_reference_latency  # category: measured (Jetson AI Lab, INT4 on AGX Orin)
    s_three_cameras = 800  # category: illustrative; three views plus prompt and state tokens

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    m_fp16 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_fp16)
    m_int4 = RM.intent_weight_memory
    b_sus = (b_peak * eta).to(GB / second)
    ridge = (pi_fp16 / b_peak).to(flop / byte)
    intensity_prefill = (2 * n_params.to(count).magnitude * s_in * flop / (m_fp16)).to(flop / byte)

    fp16 = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_fp16,
        s_in,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    int4 = RM.intent_latency_breakdown
    int4_parallel = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_int4,
        s_in,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        parallel_decode=True,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    int4_three = calc_vla_inference_latency(
        n_params,
        m_int4,
        s_three_cameras,
        d_action,
        pi_fp16,
        b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=eta,
        compute_utilization=u,
        n_layers=n_layers,
        hidden_dim=d_model,
    )
    t_sweep_fp16 = fp16["t_weight_sweep"]
    f_wall = (1 / t_sweep_fp16).to(hertz)
    flops_linear = (2 * n_params.to(count).magnitude * s_in) * flop
    flops_attn = (2 * n_layers * d_model * s_in**2) * flop
    t_prefill = int4["t_prefill"]
    t_int4 = RM.intent_inference_latency
    f_int4 = int4["f_max"]
    rate = RM.intent_rate
    t_period = (1 / rate).to(millisecond)
    t_period_next = (1 / (rate + 1 * hertz)).to(millisecond)
    t_period_5hz = (1 / (5 * hertz)).to(millisecond)
    measured_gap = abs((t_int4 - t_measured) / t_measured).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    parallel_slack = ((t_period_5hz - int4_parallel["t_total"]) / t_period_5hz).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(m_fp16.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 1e-9, f"FP16 weights drifted: {m_fp16}")
    check(abs(t_sweep_fp16.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 5e-3, f"FP16 sweep drifted: {t_sweep_fp16}")
    check(abs(f_wall.magnitude - 10.20) < 5e-3, f"Memory-wall rate drifted: {f_wall}")
    check(s_in == 288 and d_action == 7, f"Intent tokens drifted: {s_in}, {d_action}")
    check(intensity_prefill > ridge, "Prefill intensity must exceed the ridge (compute-bound)")
    check(fp16["prefill_bound"] == "compute" and int4["prefill_bound"] == "compute", "Prefill must be compute-bound")
    check(abs(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude - 188.55) < 5e-3, f"Prefill drifted: {t_prefill}")
    check(int4["t_prefill"] == fp16["t_prefill"], "Weight-only quantization must not change the prefill")
    check(abs(fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 776.78) < 5e-3, f"FP16 total drifted: {fp16['t_total']}")
    check(abs(t_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"INT4 total drifted: {t_int4}")
    check(measured_gap < 0.05, f"Model must stay near the measured INT4 latency: {measured_gap}")
    check(abs(rate.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {rate}")
    check(t_period >= t_int4 > t_period_next, "Rate must be the largest whole-hertz rate the latency supports")
    check(t_int4 > t_period_5hz, "A 5 Hz intent rate must be infeasible at the deployed configuration")
    check(0 < parallel_slack < 0.05, f"Parallel decoding must fit 5 Hz only with thin slack: {parallel_slack}")
    check(abs(int4_three["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 675.8) < 0.05, f"Three-camera case drifted: {int4_three['t_total']}")
    # margin_intent_prefill_decode_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 189, 588, 147, 777, 336, and 500 ms.
    check(
        [round(x.to(millisecond).magnitude) for x in (t_prefill, fp16["t_decode"], int4["t_decode"], t_period)] == [189, 588, 147, 500],
        "Envelope margin labels drifted",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(n_params, precision=0)
    n_layers_str = fmt_int(n_layers)
    d_model_str = fmt_int(d_model, commas=False)
    d_action_str = fmt_int(d_action)
    decode_steps_str = fmt_int(int4["decode_steps"])
    s_in_str = fmt_int(s_in)
    patches_str = fmt_int(patches)
    prompt_tokens_str = fmt_int(s_in - patches)
    _u_display = f"{u:g}"
    pi_str = fmt_qty(pi_fp16, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=0)
    u_pct_str = fmt_percent(u, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    eta_pct_str = fmt_percent(eta, precision=0, style="prose")
    b_sus_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sus, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    m_fp16_str = fmt_memory(m_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    m_int4_str = fmt_memory(m_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge, precision=1)
    intensity_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(intensity_prefill, precision=0)
    sweep_fp16_str = fmt_latency(t_sweep_fp16, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int4_str = fmt_latency(int4["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_wall_str = fmt_frequency(f_wall, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    prefill_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_prefill, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    prefill_whole_str = fmt_latency(round(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    decode_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(fp16["t_decode"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    decode_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(int4["t_decode"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    total_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_fp16_str = fmt_frequency(fp16["f_max"], unit=hertz, precision=1)
    total_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(t_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_int4_str = fmt_frequency(f_int4, unit=hertz, precision=2)
    t_measured_str = fmt_latency(t_measured, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    measured_gap_str = fmt_percent(measured_gap, precision=1, style="prose")
    rate_str = fmt_frequency(rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    rate_next_str = fmt_frequency(rate + 1 * hertz, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    period_next_str = fmt_latency(round(t_period_next.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    period_5hz_str = fmt_latency(t_period_5hz, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    rate_5hz_str = fmt_frequency(1 / t_period_5hz, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    parallel_tokens_str = fmt_int(int4_parallel["prefill_tokens"])
    parallel_total_str = fmt_latency(round(int4_parallel["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    parallel_slack_str = fmt_percent(parallel_slack, precision=1, style="prose")
    s_three_str = fmt_int(s_three_cameras)
    three_total_str = fmt_latency(round(int4_three["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)

    sweep_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{sweep}}}} = \frac{{M_{{\text{{weights}}}}}}{{\text{{BW}}_{{\text{{mem}}}}}} = \frac{{{m_fp16_str}}}{{{b_sus_str}}} \approx {sweep_fp16_str}, \qquad f \le \frac{{1}}{{t_{{\text{{sweep}}}}}} \approx {f_wall_str}"
    )
    flops_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"O_{{\text{{prefill}}}} \approx 2 N S + 2 N_{{L}} d S^2 = {sci_latex(flops_linear, precision=2)} + {sci_latex(flops_attn, precision=2)} \approx {sci_latex(int4['prefill_flops'], precision=2)}\ \text{{FLOP}}"
    )
    prefill_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{prefill}}}} = \frac{{O_{{\text{{prefill}}}}}}{{\eta_{{\text{{hw}}}}\,R_{{\text{{peak}}}}}} = \frac{{{sci_latex(int4['prefill_flops'], precision=2)}\ \text{{FLOP}}}}{{{_u_display} \times {pi_str}}} \approx {prefill_ms_str}"
    )
    fp16_total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{FP16}}}} = t_{{\text{{prefill}}}} + (S_{{\text{{out}}}}-1)\,t_{{\text{{sweep}}}} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_steps_str} \times {sweep_fp16_str} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_fp16_str} = {total_fp16_str}"
    )
    int4_total_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{INT4}}}} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_steps_str} \times {sweep_int4_str} \approx {prefill_whole_str} + {decode_int4_str} = {total_int4_str}, \qquad f \le {f_int4_str}"
    )

IntentModelLatency.u_display = IntentModelLatency._u_display
```

Consider a robot that generates continuous motor actions one discrete step at a time through an autoregressive foundation model, such as a multi-billion-parameter VLA. Its weights are *nonresident*, too large to stay in on-chip memory, so each token step streams them across the external DRAM bus. In single-token decoding with FP16 weights and request batch size $\BatchSize = 1$, the dense weight projections become matrix-vector operations ($\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$), in which each fetched weight takes part in a single multiply-add before it is discarded. The bus, not the arithmetic, then sets the pace.
