The sustained memory bandwidth $\SustainedMemoryBandwidth$ and model weight footprint $\WeightMemoryWeights$ bound the maximum fresh-evaluation frequency, as @eq-brain-memory-wall states:
$$f \le \frac{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}{\WeightMemoryWeights}$$ {#eq-brain-memory-wall}
This bound must use the bandwidth actually available to the policy and the weights it transfers at the selected precision. It prices only the weight transfer. A fresh evaluation first reads its input tokens (image patches and the instruction) through the backbone in one pass, the **prefill**\index{Prefill!compute-bound phase}, and that pass reuses every fetched weight across all of those tokens, so arithmetic rather than bandwidth can bind it. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency} prices both terms for the mobile manipulator's intent model. When a decoder emits one token per action dimension, each action dimension requires another token; if each token revisits off-chip parameters, that decode latency scales linearly with degrees of freedom.

[Single-token decoding at batch size 1]{.heading-3-inline}
Servers can combine independent requests so that a weight matrix multiplies several input vectors at once, reusing fetched weights. A robot waiting for its next action token often has only one such request. Waiting for future observations to form a batch would add delay, and sequentially dependent action tokens cannot all be evaluated at once by an autoregressive decoder. This limits reuse in those projections. It does not make every operation in an embodied model a matrix-vector product. Image patches, multiple camera views, prompt tokens, and parallel action decoders can expose matrix-matrix work within one robot's request. The one-use-per-fetch estimate therefore describes the single-token weight sweep, not the complete perception-and-action workload.

Whether a phase of the evaluation meets the memory wall or the arithmetic limit is decided by how much work it does per byte it moves, its **arithmetic intensity**\index{Arithmetic intensity!roofline} ($\ArithmeticIntensity$), defined in @eq-brain-arithmetic-intensity as:
$$\ArithmeticIntensity = \frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{Bytes transferred from off-chip memory}}$$ {#eq-brain-arithmetic-intensity}
For the dense weight projections of single-token decoding at batch size 1, each a matrix-vector product $\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{W}\mathbf{x}$, counting weight traffic alone gives an optimistic estimate, because activation and context traffic add further bytes. In FP16 each weight occupies 2 bytes and participates in exactly one multiply-accumulate operation (2 FLOPs), so
$$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2\,\text{FLOPs}}{2\,\text{Bytes}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$$
The roofline model [@williams2009roofline] turns that ratio into a bound (@fig-patterson-roofline). It plots attainable throughput against arithmetic intensity as two roofs. Below a crossover, the ridge point, throughput is capped by a sloped roof equal to bandwidth times the intensity; above it, by a flat roof equal to the processor's peak arithmetic rate. It is read the same way as the stopping-budget plot of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline, where delay travel and braking travel trade dominance at a crossover speed; both plots show two regimes and the point at which one gives way to the other.

::: {#fig-patterson-roofline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative embodied roofline**: Arithmetic intensity (operations per byte moved from off-chip memory, @eq-brain-arithmetic-intensity) against attainable throughput using the application processor's dense FP16 GPU ceiling and rounded peak memory bandwidth. Single-token weight streaming sits deep in the memory-bound region, while the intent model's prefill, which reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens, lies past the ridge, the intensity at which the bandwidth roof meets the compute roof, where compute binds. Chunk length alone does not determine arithmetic intensity; chunked workloads require measured operations and memory traffic. A separate real-time loop executes accepted waypoints between fresh model updates." fig-alt="Illustrative roofline diagram plotting arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput, with a single-token weight-streaming point on the sloped memory-bound roof, an intent-model prefill point on the flat compute-bound roof, and a ridge separating the two bounds."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ EMBODIED ROOFLINE (FIGURE)
# │ Context: @fig-patterson-roofline, placed after the arithmetic-intensity
# │          and roofline prose of @sec-brain-memory-wall that it illustrates
# │ Goal:    show single-token decode inside the memory-bound regime and the
# │          intent model's prefill past the ridge
# │ Show:    arithmetic intensity against attainable throughput for an edge part
# │ How:     roof from the registry node; one point represents an FP16
# │          matrix-vector weight sweep, excluding other memory traffic; the
# │          other the intent model's prefill (intensity ~ S, from
# │          calc-brain-intent-model-latency, which therefore runs first)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_qty, fmt_arithmetic_intensity, fmt_percent, fmt_display_math, check
from mlsysim.core.units import flop, byte

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

# ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────────────
soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet; the mobile manipulator's application processor
# Select dense FP16 GPU throughput; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating is incompatible.
node = soc.model_copy(update={"compute": soc.compute.model_copy(update={"peak_flops": soc.compute.precision_flops["fp16"]})})
I_TOKEN = 1.0  # category: illustrative; FLOP/byte for a single-token weight sweep

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
peak = node.compute.peak_flops.to("TFLOPs/s").magnitude
bw = node.memory.bandwidth.to("GB/s").magnitude
ridge = peak / (bw / 1000)  # FLOP/byte
attainable = lambda ai: min(bw * ai / 1000, peak)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 2026-09-28: prevent aggregate sparse INT8 TOPS from entering an FP16 roofline.
check(peak == 43, f"Unexpected dense FP16 roof: {peak}")
check(node.compute.peak_flops < soc.compute.peak_flops, "FP16 roof must not use aggregate INT8 TOPS")
check(abs(ridge - 210.7843) < 0.001, f"Unexpected dense FP16 ridge: {ridge}")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
roof_peak_str = fmt_qty(node.compute.peak_flops, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=0)
roof_bw_str = fmt_qty(node.memory.bandwidth, unit="GB/s", precision=0)
roof_tdp_str = fmt_qty(soc.tdp_max, unit="W", precision=0)  # datasheet: power mode the roofs assume
roof_tdp_min_str = fmt_qty(soc.tdp_min, unit="W", precision=0)  # datasheet: lowest power mode
roof_ridge_str = fmt_arithmetic_intensity(ridge * flop / byte, precision=1)
roof_attainable_str = fmt_qty(attainable(I_TOKEN) * node.compute.peak_flops.units, unit="TFLOPs/s", precision=3)
roof_fraction_str = fmt_percent(attainable(I_TOKEN) / peak, precision=2, style="prose")
roof_ridge_display_math = fmt_display_math(
    rf"I_{{\text{{ridge}}}} = \frac{{R_{{\text{{peak}}}}}}{{\text{{BW}}}} = \frac{{{roof_peak_str}}}{{{roof_bw_str}}} \approx {roof_ridge_str}"
)

points = [
    ("Autoregressive VLA\n(single token)", I_TOKEN),
    (f"Intent-model prefill\n(S = {IntentModelLatency.s_in} tokens)", IntentModelLatency.intensity_prefill.to(flop / byte).magnitude),
]

# ┌── 5. PLOT ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = viz.plot_roofline(node)
COLORS = viz.COLORS
ax.set_ylim(peak * 0.0004, peak * 2)  # keep the single-token point on scale
# Vol IV roles: the ridge is a structural fact, not a hazard, so it is drawn in
# ink rather than red; the two proposer workloads use the proposal role (bronze).
INK, PROPOSAL = "#1A202C", "#B87333"
for ln in ax.lines:
    if ln.get_marker() == "D":
        ln.set_color(INK)
    elif ln.get_linestyle() == ":":
        ln.set_color("#4A5568")
for t in ax.texts:
    s = t.get_text()
    if s.startswith("Ridge Point"):
        # move the ridge label into the empty space above the sloped roof,
        # clear of the prefill point that sits just past the ridge
        t.set_color(INK)
        t.xyann = (ridge * 0.12, peak * 0.55)
        t.arrow_patch.set_color(INK)
    elif s.startswith("MEMORY"):
        t.set_position((t.get_position()[0], peak * 0.008))  # below the roof line, clear of the ridge annotation
for idx, (label, ai) in enumerate(points):
    y = attainable(ai)
    ax.plot(ai, y, "o", ms=8, color=PROPOSAL, zorder=11)
    # the lowest point has no room beneath the roof, so its label goes above
    if idx == 0:
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 0.30, y * 4.0), "left", "bottom"
    else:
        # the prefill point sits just past the ridge; its label drops into the compute-bound region
        pos, ha, va = (ai * 2.5, y * 0.25), "left", "top"
    ax.annotate(
        label,
        xy=(ai, y),
        xytext=pos,
        fontsize=8,
        color=PROPOSAL,
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        zorder=11,
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=PROPOSAL, lw=0.9),  # leader in the label's proposal role
    )

# the reuse a workload would need before it left the memory-bound regime
ax.annotate(
    f"intensity must reach {ridge:.0f} FLOP/byte\nbefore compute binds",
    xy=(ridge, peak * 0.006),
    xytext=(ridge * 0.30, peak * 0.0012),
    fontsize=8,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    ha="right",
    zorder=11,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9),
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The mobile manipulator's application processor is a Jetson AGX Orin module (@sec-appendix-systems-machine-data-sheet). In its `{python} roof_tdp_str` maximum-performance power mode, its dense FP16 GPU Tensor Core ceiling is `{python} roof_peak_str`; the aggregate sparse INT8 rating cannot be used for this FP16 workload. Using the registry's rounded peak memory bandwidth of `{python} roof_bw_str`, the hardware ridge point occurs at:
`{python} roof_ridge_display_math`
For this weight-streaming example, $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0\,\text{FLOP/byte}$ is far below `{python} roof_ridge_str`, so memory bandwidth sets the roofline ceiling. Attainable throughput is bounded by the peak bandwidth times $I_{\text{token}}$, or `{python} roof_attainable_str`, about `{python} roof_fraction_str` of the dense FP16 peak; the sustained bandwidth that the notebook below uses lowers it further. That ratio is a workload throughput bound, not a measurement of how many cores are idle. Both roofs also assume the maximum-performance mode. A battery-powered base often runs a lower power mode, down to `{python} roof_tdp_min_str` on this module, where lower clocks drop both the compute and the bandwidth roof; the chassis thermal budget sets the mode the machine can sustain.

::: {#dfn-brain-memory-wall .callout-definition title="Memory wall"}

***Memory wall***\index{Memory wall!definition} is the limit on a workload's rate that arises when its operands cannot reach the arithmetic units as fast as those units could consume them, so that the bytes moved from off-chip memory, not the operations performed, set the time per evaluation.

1.  **Significance**: A proposer whose weights do not stay on chip must stream them at least once per fresh evaluation, which gives @eq-brain-memory-wall. On the machine's application processor, the intent model's `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str` of FP16 weights at `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_sus_str` sustained allow at most `{python} IntentModelLatency.f_wall_str` before any vision or decoding work, two orders of magnitude below the `{python} TwoSpeedRates.f_tick_str` permission tick.
2.  **Distinction**: A compute bound yields to faster arithmetic; the memory wall yields only to fewer bytes per evaluation (fewer or narrower weights, or weights that stay resident on chip) or to more bandwidth. It is also distinct from memory capacity: a model can fit in DRAM and still be too slow to stream.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that a processor's peak arithmetic rating predicts its batch-1 inference rate. Single-token weight streaming on this processor reaches only about `{python} roof_fraction_str` of its dense FP16 peak, so the rating overstates the attainable rate by orders of magnitude.

:::

On the mobile manipulator's application processor, then, the memory wall[^fn-memory-wall-cadence] caps the intent model's fresh-evaluation rate, before any vision or decoding work, far below the 100–1000 Hz at which stabilization, joint impedance control, and reflex-level collision avoidance run (notebook \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}). A model renewed that slowly can say where the arm should go, but it cannot close the loop on moving mass, so it proposes waypoints and a faster loop below it tracks them. That conclusion is about timing only. The separate requirement that learned outputs remain proposals, even when they arrive in time, comes from the failures of @sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities.

[^fn-memory-wall-cadence]: **Wulf and McKee**\index{Memory wall!origin}: Their short paper named the memory wall [@wulf1995], observing that processor speed was improving far faster than DRAM latency, so that memory access would eventually dominate run time whatever the processor did. Caches postponed the wall for workloads that reuse their data, but a batch-1 model on a robot meets it directly. When each weight is used once per fetch, the bus, not the arithmetic, sets how often a fresh proposal can arrive.

Repeated off-chip transfers also consume memory-system energy. Their power cost depends on the DRAM, controller, access pattern, and transfer rate, so a bandwidth calculation alone does not establish battery drain or actuator heating. Whatever the processor dissipates is heat released inside the same sealed chassis as the joint motors, and it raises the ambient temperature against which @sec-body-thermal-capacity rates each motor's continuous torque.

A fresh evaluation is not a single point on the roofline. Its prefill reuses each fetched weight across all of its input tokens and lands past the ridge, while its decode returns to the memory-bound point, one full weight sweep per token. For a decoder that emits $\EmittedTokenCountOut$ tokens one after another, @eq-brain-eval-latency adds the two phases:
$$\ProposerInferenceTime \approx \max\!\left(\frac{O_{\text{prefill}}}{\EfficiencyHw\,\PeakRate},\ \frac{\WeightMemoryWeights}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}\right) + (\EmittedTokenCountOut-1)\,\frac{\WeightMemoryWeights}{\SustainedMemoryBandwidth}$$ {#eq-brain-eval-latency}
Here $O_{\text{prefill}}$ counts the prefill's operations, $\PeakRate$ is the processor's peak arithmetic rate at the activation precision, and $\EfficiencyHw$ is the fraction of that rate the prefill achieves. The prefill cannot finish before its own weight sweep, hence the maximum; the prefill emits the first token, and each of the other $\EmittedTokenCountOut - 1$ tokens costs one more sweep. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency} prices both phases for the machine's intent model.

::: {#nbk-brain-intent-model-latency .callout-notebook title="Pricing one intent-model evaluation"}

**Problem**: The mobile manipulator's intent model is a `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str`-parameter vision-language model sized after OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], running on the application processor. Where OpenVLA decodes a step of end-effector motion, the machine's model decodes the same number of tokens to name a target pose (@sec-brain-proposer-interface). How long does one fresh evaluation take, which resource binds each part of it, and what renewal rate can the machine therefore state?

**Variables**:

* Parameters $N =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str` in $\NumberOfLayers =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.n_layers_str` layers of width $\HiddenDimension =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_model_str` (Datasheet). The decoder emits $\EmittedTokenCountOut =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_action_str` tokens, one per output dimension, one after another (Datasheet).
* Input tokens $\SequenceLength =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.s_in_str`: `{python} IntentModelLatency.patches_str` patches from one $224{\times}224$ view (Derived) plus `{python} IntentModelLatency.prompt_tokens_str` instruction tokens (Illustrative).
* Dense FP16 peak $\PeakRate =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.pi_str` (Datasheet), of which the prefill achieves $\EfficiencyHw =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.u_pct_str` (Illustrative).
* Peak bandwidth `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_peak_str` (Datasheet), of which `{python} IntentModelLatency.eta_pct_str` is sustained (Illustrative), so $\SustainedMemoryBandwidth =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_sus_str`.
* Stored weights: FP16 (2 bytes per parameter) or INT4 (half a byte), with activations kept in 16 bits (Chosen).

**Math**:

*The memory wall.* FP16 weights occupy `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str`. If every evaluation streams them once, the bound above gives
`{python} IntentModelLatency.sweep_display_math`

*The prefill binds on arithmetic.* All $\SequenceLength$ input tokens pass through the backbone together, costing two FLOPs per parameter per token (each weight multiplies one input value and adds the product to a running sum) plus a small attention term:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.flops_display_math`
Each fetched weight now serves $\SequenceLength$ tokens, so the intensity is about $\SequenceLength \approx$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.intensity_str`, beyond the `{python} IntentModelLatency.ridge_str` ridge of @fig-patterson-roofline. Arithmetic binds, and the weight sweep runs underneath it:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_display_math`

*The decode binds on bandwidth.* The prefill emits the first action token. Each of the remaining $\EmittedTokenCountOut - 1 =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.decode_steps_str` tokens is a matrix-vector pass that rereads every weight:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.fp16_total_display_math`
That is about `{python} IntentModelLatency.f_fp16_str`.

*INT4 weights shrink only the bandwidth term.* Storing the weights in four bits cuts them to `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_int4_str` and each sweep to `{python} IntentModelLatency.sweep_int4_str`, but the prefill still multiplies 16-bit activations at the FP16 rate:
`{python} IntentModelLatency.int4_total_display_math`

*Sensitivity.* Parallel decoding [@kim2025openvlaoft] moves the action tokens into the prefill ($\SequenceLength + \EmittedTokenCountOut =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_tokens_str`) and removes the decode sweeps, giving `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_total_str`, only `{python} IntentModelLatency.parallel_slack_str` inside a `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_5hz_str` period with the processor busy for all of it. Three camera views ($\SequenceLength \approx$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.s_three_str`) raise the INT4 total to `{python} IntentModelLatency.three_total_str`.

**Result**: At INT4 one evaluation takes about `{python} IntentModelLatency.total_int4_str`. A published measurement of the same model and quantization on this processor reports `{python} IntentModelLatency.t_measured_str` per frame [@franklin2024openvla], a gap of `{python} IntentModelLatency.measured_gap_str`. That agreement is closer than two illustrative factors deserve. It shows that the model has the right terms, not that $\EfficiencyHw$ and the sustained fraction are exactly right. A `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_next_str` rate would need a `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_next_str` period, so the machine runs its intent model at `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_str`, one evaluation per `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_str`.

**Systems insight**: The binding resource depends on the phase. Prefill reuses weights across tokens and is compute-bound; decode rereads them per token and is bandwidth-bound [@pope2023efficiently]. Weight-only quantization attacks only the second, so after INT4 the compute-bound prefill is most of the latency, and the next gain must come from fewer input tokens, lower-precision arithmetic that the processor's kernels support, or a faster compute roof. @Sec-brain-quantization develops that choice and its accuracy cost.

:::

### Quantizing the intent model {#sec-brain-quantization}

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-quantization
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WEIGHT-ONLY QUANTIZATION OF THE INTENT MODEL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-brain-quantization and @tbl-03-intent-quantization
# │ Goal:    price the intent model at FP16, 8-bit, and INT4 weights against
# │          the published measurements on the same module, and show the
# │          prefill ceiling no weight-only format can pass
# │ Show:    777 / 483 / 336 ms computed vs 840 / 471 / 336 ms measured;
# │          prefill 56 percent of INT4 latency; 5.3 Hz weight-only ceiling;
# │          3.1 percent scale overhead at g = 128
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency at each bytes-per-parameter
# │          (weight-only: prefill unchanged); f_ceiling = 1 / t_prefill
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_memory, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, fmt_percent, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _q_latency(bytes_per_param):
    """Prefill-plus-decode latency of the intent model at one weight precision."""
    L = IntentModelLatency
    return calc_vla_inference_latency(
        L.n_params,
        memory_from_params(L.n_params, bytes_per_param),
        L.s_in,
        L.d_action,
        L.pi_fp16,
        L.b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=L.eta,
        compute_utilization=L.u,
        n_layers=L.n_layers,
        hidden_dim=L.d_model,
    )

class IntentQuantization:
    """The intent model at three weight precisions, computed against measured."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    n_params = IntentModelLatency.n_params  # category: datasheet
    bpp_fp16 = 2.0 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen
    bpp_int8 = 1.0 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (8-bit weights, 16-bit arithmetic)
    bpp_int4 = RM.intent_weight_bytes_per_param  # category: chosen (deployed)
    # Jetson AI Lab, OpenVLA-7B on AGX Orin 64GB, JetPack 6 (prov:jetson-ai-lab-openvla-orin):
    # mean per-frame latency and action-prediction accuracy on BridgeData V2 episodes that
    # were part of OpenVLA's training data (re-verified 2026-09-29). The page labels the
    # 8-bit row "FP8", but its command runs MLC's q8f16_ft mode: 8-bit weights, FP16 compute.
    meas_fp16 = 840 * millisecond  # category: measured (Hugging Face runtime)
    meas_int8 = 471 * millisecond  # category: measured (q8f16_ft, MLC runtime)
    meas_int4 = RM.intent_reference_latency  # category: measured
    acc_fp16, acc_int8, acc_int4 = 0.953, 0.952, 0.901  # category: measured
    # Kim et al. 2024 (OpenVLA), Table 2: real-robot task success on a desktop GPU
    ovla_bf16, ovla_int8, ovla_int4 = 0.713, 0.581, 0.719  # category: literature
    # Kim et al. 2024, Sec. 5.3: int8 ran at 1.2 Hz on the A5000 evaluation GPU, against
    # the 5 Hz control rate of the training data; the authors attribute the drop to that
    ovla_int8_rate, ovla_train_rate = 1.2 * hertz, 5 * hertz  # category: literature
    group = 128  # category: literature (AWQ group size, Lin et al. 2024, Sec. 5.1)
    scale_bits = 16  # category: chosen (one FP16 scale per group)
    weight_bits = 4  # category: chosen (INT4)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    r_fp16, r_int8, r_int4 = _q_latency(bpp_fp16), _q_latency(bpp_int8), _q_latency(bpp_int4)
    mem_fp16 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_fp16).to(GB)
    mem_int8 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_int8).to(GB)
    mem_int4 = memory_from_params(n_params, bpp_int4).to(GB)
    gap_fp16 = ((r_fp16["t_total"] - meas_fp16) / meas_fp16).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    gap_int8 = ((r_int8["t_total"] - meas_int8) / meas_int8).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    gap_int4 = ((r_int4["t_total"] - meas_int4) / meas_int4).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_prefill = r_int4["t_prefill"]
    prefill_share = (t_prefill / r_int4["t_total"]).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    f_ceiling = (1 / t_prefill).to(hertz)
    scale_overhead = (scale_bits / group) / weight_bits

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(r_fp16["t_prefill"] == r_int8["t_prefill"] == t_prefill, "Weight-only formats must share one prefill")
    check(abs(r_int8["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude - 482.66) < 0.01, f"8-bit total drifted: {r_int8['t_total']}")
    check(abs((r_int4["t_total"] - IntentModelLatency.t_int4).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-6, "INT4 row must match the notebook")
    check(abs(gap_int8) < 0.03 and abs(gap_int4) < 0.01, f"Computed must track measured: {gap_int8}, {gap_int4}")
    check(-0.09 < gap_fp16 < -0.06, f"FP16 underestimate drifted: {gap_fp16}")
    check(0.55 < prefill_share < 0.57, f"Prefill share drifted: {prefill_share}")
    check(5.0 < f_ceiling.magnitude < 5.4, f"Weight-only ceiling drifted: {f_ceiling}")
    check(f_ceiling > RM.intent_rate, "The deployed rate must sit below the weight-only ceiling")
    check(abs(scale_overhead - 0.03125) < 1e-12, f"Scale overhead drifted: {scale_overhead}")
    check(ovla_int8_rate < ovla_train_rate, "The int8 run must be slower than the training control rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    bpp_fp16_str = fmt_int(bpp_fp16.magnitude)
    bpp_int8_str = fmt_int(bpp_int8.magnitude)
    bpp_int4_str = fmt(bpp_int4.magnitude, precision=1)
    mem_fp16_str = fmt_memory(mem_fp16, unit=GB, precision=0)
    mem_int8_str = fmt_memory(mem_int8, unit=GB, precision=0)
    mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
    sweep_fp16_str = fmt_latency(r_fp16["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int8_str = fmt_latency(r_int8["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    sweep_int4_str = fmt_latency(r_int4["t_weight_sweep"], unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    pred_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(r_fp16["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pred_int8_str = fmt_latency(round(r_int8["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pred_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(r_int4["t_total"].to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_fp16_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_fp16.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_int8_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_int8.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    meas_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(meas_int4.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    acc_fp16_str = fmt_percent(acc_fp16, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_int8_str = fmt_percent(acc_int8, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_int4_str = fmt_percent(acc_int4, precision=1, style="symbol")
    acc_fp16_prose_str = fmt_percent(acc_fp16, precision=1, style="prose")
    acc_int4_prose_str = fmt_percent(acc_int4, precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_16_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_fp16), precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_8_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_int8), precision=1, style="prose")
    gap_4_str = fmt_percent(abs(gap_int4), precision=1, style="prose")
    prefill_share_str = fmt_percent(round(prefill_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    f_ceiling_str = fmt_frequency(f_ceiling, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    group_str = fmt_int(group)
    scale_overhead_pct_str = fmt_percent(scale_overhead, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_bf16_str = fmt_percent(ovla_bf16, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int8_str = fmt_percent(ovla_int8, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int4_str = fmt_percent(ovla_int4, precision=1, style="prose")
    ovla_int8_rate_str = fmt_frequency(ovla_int8_rate, unit=hertz, precision=1)
    ovla_train_rate_str = fmt_frequency(ovla_train_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
```

The memory wall leaves two levers on the weight term, fewer weights or fewer bytes per weight. A smaller model gives up the recognition the intent model exists to supply, so the machine keeps the `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str`-parameter model and pulls the second lever. **Quantization**\index{Quantization!weight-only} stores each weight as a low-precision integer plus a shared scale, and reconstructs an approximate weight when the kernel needs it. In the common symmetric form, the weights are divided into groups of $g$, each group keeps one 16-bit scale $s$, and each weight $w_i$ becomes a $b$-bit integer $q_i$ [@jacob2018quantization; @lin2024awq]:
$$s = \frac{\max_{i \in \text{group}} |w_i|}{2^{b-1} - 1}, \qquad q_i = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{w_i}{s}\right),\, -2^{b-1},\, 2^{b-1} - 1\right), \qquad \hat{w}_i = s\, q_i$$
Rounding moves each reconstructed weight $\hat{w}_i$ at most $s/2$ from $w_i$, so one large weight in a group coarsens the step for all the others; choosing which weights to protect from that error is where quantization methods differ. The stored size is $b/8$ bytes per weight plus the scales' share. At $b = 4$ with the `{python} IntentQuantization.group_str`-weight groups that activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) uses [@lin2024awq], the scales add `{python} IntentQuantization.scale_overhead_pct_str` to the four-bit payload, which the half-byte-per-parameter figure used here leaves out.

Two families of quantization act on different terms of the latency. *Weight-only* quantization, the machine's choice, restores each weight to 16 bits inside the kernel just before the multiply. It shrinks the bytes every decode sweep rereads, but the arithmetic still runs at the 16-bit rate, so the compute-bound prefill does not move. *Weight-and-activation* quantization makes both operands integers, so the multiplications themselves run on integer units and can shorten the prefill as well. It pays off only when three conditions hold: the processor has fast integer units for that precision, the runtime has kernels for the model's layer shapes, and the activations tolerate the coarser grid. A format without a kernel is only a smaller file.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_intent_prefill_decode_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two stacked horizontal bars against a dashed 500 millisecond period line. FP16: a 189 milliseconds prefill segment plus a 588 milliseconds decode segment, 777 ms in total, crossing the period line. INT4: the same 189 milliseconds prefill plus a 147 milliseconds decode, 336 ms in total, inside the period."}

*INT4 shrinks the decode; the `{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_whole_str` prefill it cannot touch now dominates.*
:::

@Tbl-03-intent-quantization prices the intent model at three weight precisions with the prefill-plus-decode model of notebook \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}, beside measurements of the same model on the same module [@franklin2024openvla].

| Weight format   |                        Bytes per parameter |                                    Weights |                                 Weight sweep |                            Computed latency |                            Measured latency |                 Action-prediction accuracy |
|:----------------|-------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|---------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|--------------------------------------------:|-------------------------------------------:|
| FP16            | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_fp16_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_fp16_str` |
| 8-bit           | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_int8_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int8_str` |
| INT4 (deployed) | `{python} IntentQuantization.bpp_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.sweep_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.pred_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.meas_int4_str` | `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int4_str` |

: **Weight-only quantization of the intent model**: Computed latency uses the sustained bandwidth and the illustrative prefill utilization of @sec-brain-memory-wall; measured latency and action-prediction accuracy are the Jetson AI Lab means over BridgeData V2 episodes on the 64 GB Jetson AGX Orin module [@franklin2024openvla]. The episodes were part of the model's training data, so the accuracy column measures how faithfully each format reproduces the FP16 model, not how well it generalizes. The source labels its 8-bit build FP8, but runs it in a mode that stores 8-bit weights and computes in 16 bits, the same weight-only form the computed row assumes. The FP16 measurement used a general-purpose runtime (Hugging Face) rather than the optimized one (MLC) used for the other two. {#tbl-03-intent-quantization tbl-colwidths="[16,12,12,12,16,16,16]"}

The computed and measured columns agree within `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_8_str` for the 8-bit format and `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_4_str` for INT4. The model underestimates the FP16 run by `{python} IntentQuantization.gap_16_str`, consistent with that run's slower runtime, so the comparison supports the model's two terms rather than its exact constants. The table also shows where weight-only quantization stops paying. Each halving of the bytes halves the sweep, but the `{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_ms_str` prefill is untouched, and at INT4 it is already `{python} IntentQuantization.prefill_share_str` of the latency. Even weights that cost no bytes at all would leave the prefill, so no weight-only format can lift the intent model above `{python} IntentQuantization.f_ceiling_str`. Beyond that ceiling, the gain must come from integer arithmetic in the prefill, fewer input tokens, or a processor with a higher compute roof.

The last column carries the cost. On this module the INT4 build's action-prediction accuracy fell from `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_fp16_prose_str` to `{python} IntentQuantization.acc_int4_prose_str` [@franklin2024openvla]. OpenVLA's authors, measuring task success on a real robot with a desktop GPU, found a different pattern. INT4 weights kept `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int4_str` success against `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_bf16_str` for bfloat16, while INT8 weights through a general-purpose quantization library fell to `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int8_str`. The cause was time, not rounding. The library's added quantization operations cost more than the saved bytes, so the INT8 policy ran at `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_int8_rate_str` on the evaluation GPU, against the `{python} IntentQuantization.ovla_train_rate_str` control rate of its training data, and the robot met each observation later than the demonstrations had [@kim2024openvla]. On the module an 8-bit format was nearly free and INT4 cost accuracy; on the desktop GPU the 8-bit build lost success through its slower loop and INT4 was nearly free. The two 8-bit results used different software and kernels, and the two studies scored different tasks, so the pair shows that a bit width alone does not predict the outcome; the quantization method, the kernels, the control rate they allow, and the task together do. A quantized checkpoint is a different model. It must be evaluated on the machine's own contact tasks at the deployed precision, carry its own calibration, and be named as such by the `model_id` of the proposal payload (@sec-brain-proposer-information). The footprint saving also has a systems value. Dropping from `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_fp16_str` to `{python} IntentQuantization.mem_int4_str` of weights returns memory that retained context and perception also need. How much of the computed saving survives when the cameras and the chunk policy share the bus must be measured under load.

Quantization therefore leaves the machine's intent model at `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_str`, one fresh proposal every `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_str`, while the arm below it consumes setpoints tens of times faster. No lever on the weight term closes a gap that large, and the gap raises two questions the weights cannot answer: how the arm stays supplied between evaluations, and how long whatever supplies it stays true.

::: {#chk-brain-memory-wall-levers .callout-checkpoint title="The memory wall and its levers"}

One fresh evaluation of a large proposer pays a compute-bound prefill and a bandwidth-bound decode, and each lever moves only one of them.

- [ ] **Weight-streaming ceiling**: Given a model's parameter count, its bytes per parameter, and a sustained bandwidth, can you compute the ceiling of @eq-brain-memory-wall and say what it leaves out?
- [ ] **Prefill vs. decode**: Can you explain, from arithmetic intensity, why the intent model's prefill lands past the ridge of @fig-patterson-roofline while each decode token sits on the sloped roof?
- [ ] **Weight-only quantization**: Which term of @eq-brain-eval-latency does INT4 shrink, and why does that leave a rate ceiling that no weight-only format can pass?
- [ ] **Shorter-input estimate**: The INT4 evaluation is a `{python} IntentModelLatency.prefill_whole_str` prefill of $\SequenceLength =$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.s_in_str` tokens plus `{python} IntentModelLatency.decode_steps_str` sweeps of `{python} IntentModelLatency.sweep_int4_str`. Treating the prefill as proportional to $\SequenceLength$, estimate whether halving the input tokens would fit one evaluation inside the `{python} IntentModelLatency.period_5hz_str` period of a `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_5hz_str` rate.

:::

## Chunk Supply and Evidence Validity {#sec-brain-chunk-supply}

One INT4 evaluation of the intent model takes `{python} IntentModelLatency.total_int4_str`. Over that interval the mug keeps riding the conveyor, and an arm tracking a new setpoint every few tens of milliseconds would have nothing to track if each proposal named a single setpoint. Predicting a sequence of setpoints per evaluation solves the supply problem but raises a second one that the memory wall never touched. Every setpoint in such a sequence descends from one observation, so the sequence can outlast the evidence behind it. This section sizes the chunks the machine's two proposers supply, then asks how long that supply stays true, what the slow proposer should hand the fast one, and what a proposal must carry for the permission path to refuse it.

### Action chunking {#sec-brain-action-chunking}

The memory bound limits how often a large model can revise its proposal. A controller can track previously admitted motion between those revisions, but a policy that supplies only one future setpoint leaves little planned motion available while it computes. Predicting a trajectory segment gives the controller a sequence to track without making the next fresh observation arrive sooner.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-chunk-supply-demand
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BANDWIDTH DEMANDED BY SINGLE-STEP VERSUS CHUNKED SUPPLY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the supply-rate paragraph in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    show why one weight sweep per setpoint cannot feed the arm
# │ Show:    40 Hz x 14 GB = 560 GB/s, 3.9x the 142.8 GB/s sustained; H = 16
# │          cuts demand to 35.0 GB/s, 24.5 percent of sustained (25 ms
# │          setpoint step since M5, 2026-09-28; was 50 Hz / 700 GB/s)
# │ How:     demand = f_supply x M_weights; chunked = demand / H
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ChunkSupplyDemand:
    """Weight-sweep bandwidth demanded at the setpoint rate, single-step versus chunked."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    f_supply = (1 / RM.chunk_step).to(hertz)  # category: derived (setpoint rate)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    m_fp16 = IntentModelLatency.m_fp16  # category: derived (FP16 intent weights)
    b_sus = IntentModelLatency.b_sus  # category: derived (sustained bandwidth)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    demand = (f_supply * m_fp16).to(GB / second)
    over = (demand / b_sus).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    demand_chunk = (demand / horizon).to(GB / second)
    share_chunk = (demand_chunk / b_sus).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(f_supply.magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint rate drifted: {f_supply}")
    check(abs(demand.magnitude - 560.0) < 1e-6, f"Single-step demand drifted: {demand}")
    check(over > 1, "Single-step supply must exceed the sustained bandwidth")
    check(demand_chunk < b_sus, "Chunked supply must fit the sustained bandwidth")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply_str = fmt_frequency(f_supply, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    f_supply_num_str = fmt_int(f_supply.magnitude)
    demand_str = fmt_bandwidth(demand, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    over_str = fmt(over, precision=1)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    demand_chunk_str = fmt_bandwidth(demand_chunk, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    share_chunk_str = fmt_percent(share_chunk, precision=1, style="prose")
```

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-chunk-schedule
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE CHUNK POLICY'S RENEWAL SCHEDULE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the supply, replanning, and reaction bullets and the temporal
# │          ensembling paragraph in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    give the three rates of the selected chunk policy and show that
# │          its renewal falls on the setpoint grid
# │ Show:    40 Hz supply (25 ms step); 20 Hz / 50 ms renewal = 2 setpoints;
# │          50 + 40 = 90 ms reaction; 8 chunks cover each step (H = 16)
# │ How:     RM.chunk_schedule (calc_chunk_renewal_schedule), 2026-09-28, M5
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
import math
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ChunkSchedule:
    """Setpoint supply, renewal, and reaction timing of the machine's chunk policy."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (setpoint step)
    f_replan = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen (renewal rate)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    sched = RM.chunk_schedule  # category: derived (calc_chunk_renewal_schedule)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply = (1 / step).to(hertz)
    t_replan = sched["renewal_period"]
    n_per_renewal = sched["setpoints_per_renewal"]
    t_reaction = sched["open_loop_span"]
    n_overlap = sched["overlapping_chunks"]
    n_frozen = math.ceil((t_infer / step).to("dimensionless").magnitude)  # setpoints that execute during one inference

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(step.magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"Setpoint step drifted: {step}")
    check(abs(t_replan.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Renewal period drifted: {t_replan}")
    check(n_per_renewal == 2, f"Setpoints per renewal drifted: {n_per_renewal}")
    check(abs(t_reaction.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Reaction latency drifted: {t_reaction}")
    check(n_overlap == 8, f"Overlapping chunks drifted: {n_overlap}")
    check(n_frozen == 2 and n_frozen < horizon, f"Committed prefix drifted: {n_frozen}")
    # margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg fig-alt hand-types 16 steps, 2 past, 2 run, 12 buffer.
    check(horizon == 16 and horizon - n_frozen - n_per_renewal == 12, f"Chunk-strip margin labels drifted: H = {horizon}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    f_supply_str = fmt_frequency(f_supply, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    step_str = fmt_latency(step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    step_us_str = fmt_int(step.to(microsecond).magnitude)
    f_replan_str = fmt_frequency(f_replan, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_replan_str = fmt_latency(t_replan, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_reaction_str = fmt_latency(t_reaction, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    n_per_renewal_str = fmt_int(n_per_renewal)
    n_overlap_str = fmt_int(n_overlap)
    n_frozen_str = fmt_int(n_frozen)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
```

[Supply rate vs. closed-loop reaction latency]{.heading-3-inline}
To supply dense waypoints despite slow full-model inference, modern physical AI policies employ **action chunking**\index{Action chunking!temporal trajectory} (definition \ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) [@zhao2023learning; @chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Each chunk then crosses the proposal boundary as one packet. The transfer saving follows from reusing one evaluation across several outputs.

::: {#dfn-brain-action-chunking .callout-definition title="Temporal action chunking"}

***Temporal action chunking***\index{Temporal action chunking!definition}\index{Action chunking!definition} is the policy formulation that predicts an entire horizon of $\Horizon$ future continuous actions $\ActionChunk_{t:t+\Horizon-1} = [\mathbf{a}_t, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+\Horizon-1}]$ in a single neural evaluation or diffusion rollout, amortizing parameter memory transfers across extended physical execution windows.

1.  **Significance**: Chunking divides the weight traffic per supplied setpoint by $\Horizon$, `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str` on the mobile manipulator, but leaves the delay before a new observation can change the motion at one renewal period plus one inference, `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_reaction_str` for its chunk policy. It does not make fresh observations or policy decisions arrive at the waypoint rate; a downstream controller tracks the accepted trajectory between model updates.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike single-step policies $\mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \MultimodalObservation)$, which condition only on the current observation and re-evaluate the full neural network at every control step, action chunking deliberately generates multi-step feedforward trajectories, executing only the start of each before the next replaces it (receding-horizon execution) and blending across overlapping chunks to reconcile slow neural deliberation with fast closed-loop control.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Executing action chunks open-loop, without smoothing across chunk boundaries or a check by the permission path. Without smooth blending across overlapping chunk boundaries, switching between independently generated horizons injects acceleration jumps and torque shocks that excite mechanical gearbox resonances.

:::

Predicting a horizon[^fn-receding-horizon-control] of $\Horizon$ actions per forward pass spreads the multi-gigabyte DRAM weight streaming cost over $\Horizon \times \Delta t_{\text{step}}$ seconds of physical execution. On the mobile manipulator's application processor, a `{python} IntentModelLatency.params_str` FP16 model (`{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str`) generating single-step actions at the `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.f_supply_str` setpoint rate would demand `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.f_supply_num_str` $\times$ `{python} IntentModelLatency.m_fp16_str` $=$ `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.demand_str` of memory bandwidth, `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.over_str` times the `{python} IntentModelLatency.b_sus_str` it can sustain. A chunk of $\Horizon =$ `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.horizon_str` waypoints cuts that demand to `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.demand_chunk_str`, `{python} ChunkSupplyDemand.share_chunk_str` of the sustained bandwidth, if one sweep supplies each full chunk. More frequent replanning, decoder work, and competing memory traffic consume additional bandwidth. The saving is in weight traffic per supplied waypoint, not an equal gain in arithmetic intensity; predicting a chunk adds decoder work, and its position on the roofline depends on the operations performed and the bytes actually transferred.

[^fn-receding-horizon-control]: **Receding Horizon**\index{Receding horizon!action chunking}: Model predictive control optimizes over a fixed horizon, executes only the first part of the plan, and then replans from the newly measured state, so the horizon recedes as time advances [@mayne2000constrained]. A chunked policy is the learned analog and inherits the same rule: the unexecuted tail of a chunk is a buffer that the next evaluation may overwrite, never a commitment the machine owes to finish.

Predicting a sequence also changes how a learned policy uses recent actions, but chunking alone does not establish that the policy attends to the right evidence or recovers from an unfamiliar contact. Those properties depend on training and closed-loop evaluation. The supply calculation establishes only the weight traffic needed for the stated execution schedule.

The selected smaller policy has a separate illustrative schedule. Three quantities distinguish its setpoint supply from the delay before a new observation changes a proposal:

* *Setpoint supply cadence* ($f_{\text{supply}} = 1/\Delta t_{\text{step}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_supply_str`, $\Delta t_{\text{step}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str`): The rate at which the trajectory queue delivers discrete waypoints to the joint servo loop.
* *Policy replanning rate* ($f_{\text{replan}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_replan_str`, period $T_{\text{replan}} =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str`): The cadence at which the smaller chunk policy begins an evaluation from fresh sensory frames. The period is chosen as a whole number of setpoint steps, here `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str`, so that every renewal begins on a setpoint boundary.
* *Closed-loop reaction latency* ($T_{\text{reaction}} = T_{\text{replan}} + \ProposerInferenceTime =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` $+$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_infer_str` $=$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_reaction_str`): The worst sampling-phase wait plus the assumed inference time until a revised proposal is available, excluding further admission and physical response delay.

In this illustrative schedule, a disturbance immediately after capture can wait up to `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_reaction_str` for a revised learned proposal, before any additional admission and actuation delay. The independent permission path need not wait for that revision. Current qualified evidence, meaning measurements whose error bound and age have been established for this use (@sec-perception-error-clearance develops how), can trigger a protective response while the policy computes. Its ability to detect the relevant obstacle and complete a feasible response needs its own timing and sensing evidence. Chunking keeps candidate waypoints available; it establishes neither that response nor its deadline.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-decoder-families
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE THREE DECODER FAMILIES PRICED ON THE MACHINE'S PROCESSOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the decoder-family paragraphs in @sec-brain-action-chunking
# │ Goal:    show what one fresh H = 16 chunk costs if the intent-sized
# │          backbone produced it, for each decoder family
# │ Show:    every family pays the ~189 ms compute-bound prefill; binned
# │          autoregressive ~2.9 s, FAST (30 tokens) ~0.9 s, parallel ~0.26 s,
# │          flow expert (300M, 10 steps) ~0.24 s; none fits the 50 ms period
# │ How:     calc_vla_inference_latency (INT4 backbone) with D = H x d_a, the
# │          FAST low-end token count, or parallel decoding; expert steps are
# │          max(compute, (expert weights + prefix KV) / B_sustained)
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_memory, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _backbone(action_tokens, parallel=False):
    """The INT4 intent-sized backbone emitting action_tokens (sequential unless parallel)."""
    L = IntentModelLatency
    return calc_vla_inference_latency(
        L.n_params,
        L.m_int4,
        L.s_in,
        action_tokens,
        L.pi_fp16,
        L.b_peak,
        bus_efficiency=L.eta,
        compute_utilization=L.u,
        parallel_decode=parallel,
        n_layers=L.n_layers,
        hidden_dim=L.d_model,
    )

class DecoderFamilies:
    """One fresh H-step chunk from the intent-sized backbone, per decoder family."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (the machine's H)
    d_a = IntentModelLatency.d_action  # category: datasheet (values per action)
    fast_tokens = StateOfPractice.fast_tok_lo  # category: literature (FAST low end, Pertsch et al. 2025)
    expert_params = StateOfPractice.pi0_expert  # category: literature (pi0 action expert)
    expert_steps = StateOfPractice.pi0_steps  # category: literature (pi0 integration steps)
    expert_bpp = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen (16-bit expert weights)
    kv_per_token = (2 * IntentModelLatency.n_layers * IntentModelLatency.d_model * 2 * byte).to(MB)  # derived; full-width FP16 K and V
    b_sus = IntentModelLatency.b_sus  # category: derived
    pi_eff = IntentModelLatency.u * IntentModelLatency.pi_fp16  # category: derived (achieved FP16 rate)
    t_period = ChunkSchedule.t_replan  # category: derived (the machine's renewal period)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_binned = horizon * d_a
    r_binned = _backbone(n_binned)
    r_fast = _backbone(fast_tokens)
    r_parallel = _backbone(n_binned, parallel=True)
    r_prefill = _backbone(1)  # prefill only: the first token comes out of the prefill
    t_prefill = r_prefill["t_total"]
    expert_mem = memory_from_params(expert_params, expert_bpp).to(MB)
    prefix_kv = (kv_per_token * IntentModelLatency.s_in).to(MB)
    t_step_bw = ((expert_mem + prefix_kv) / b_sus).to(millisecond)
    t_step_compute = (2 * expert_params.to(param).magnitude * horizon * flop / pi_eff).to(millisecond)
    t_step = max(t_step_bw, t_step_compute)
    t_expert = (t_prefill + expert_steps * t_step).to(millisecond)
    t_binned, t_fast, t_parallel = r_binned["t_total"], r_fast["t_total"], r_parallel["t_total"]
    spread = (t_binned / t_expert).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_binned == 112, f"Binned token count drifted: {n_binned}")
    check(abs((t_prefill - IntentModelLatency.t_prefill).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-6, "Prefill must match the notebook")
    check(t_step_bw > t_step_compute, "Expert steps must be bandwidth-bound on this processor")
    check(t_binned > t_fast > t_parallel > t_expert > t_prefill, "Family ordering drifted")
    check(abs(t_binned.to(millisecond).magnitude - 2909.1) < 0.1, f"Binned total drifted: {t_binned}")
    check(abs(t_expert.to(millisecond).magnitude - 241.14) < 0.01, f"Expert total drifted: {t_expert}")
    check(abs(t_parallel.to(millisecond).magnitude - 264.37) < 0.01, f"Parallel total drifted: {t_parallel}")
    check(t_prefill > t_period, "The backbone prefill alone must exceed the renewal period")
    # margin_decoder_family_latency_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 2.9 s, 899, 264, 241, 189, and 50 ms.
    check(round(t_fast.to(millisecond).magnitude) == 899 and round(t_period.to(millisecond).magnitude) == 50, "Decoder ladder margin labels drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_binned_str = fmt_int(n_binned)
    fast_tokens_str = fmt_int(fast_tokens)
    t_prefill_str = fmt_latency(round(t_prefill.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_binned_str = fmt_latency(t_binned.to(second), unit=second, precision=1)
    t_fast_str = fmt_latency(round(t_fast.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_parallel_str = fmt_latency(round(t_parallel.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_expert_str = fmt_latency(round(t_expert.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    expert_mem_str = fmt_memory(expert_mem, unit=MB, precision=0)
    prefix_kv_str = fmt_memory(round(prefix_kv.magnitude) * MB, unit=MB, precision=0)
    spread_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(spread), precision=0)
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
```

[Pricing the decoder families]{.heading-3-inline}
The three decoder families of @sec-brain-learned-representations differ in how they turn one observation into a chunk, and the machine's processor prices that difference. Suppose the intent-sized backbone, with its deployed INT4 weights, produced one fresh chunk of $\Horizon =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str` setpoints of `{python} IntentModelLatency.d_action_str` values each. Every family first pays the same compute-bound prefill of the observation, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_prefill_str`, and then the families part ways:

* Binned autoregressive tokens need `{python} DecoderFamilies.n_binned_str` sequential decode steps, each rereading the backbone weights, for about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_binned_str`.
* FAST tokens cut the sequence to about `{python} DecoderFamilies.fast_tokens_str` tokens, the count its authors report per arm for a one-second chunk and therefore generous for this shorter chunk, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_fast_str`, still sequential.
* A parallel head folds every action into one longer prefill, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_parallel_str`.
* A $\pi_0$-sized action expert of `{python} DecoderFamilies.expert_mem_str` in 16-bit weights integrates `{python} StateOfPractice.pi0_steps_str` steps. Each step rereads the expert and the backbone's `{python} DecoderFamilies.prefix_kv_str` of cached keys and values rather than the backbone weights, about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_step_str` per step on bandwidth, for about `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_expert_str` in all. @Sec-appendix-ml-diffusion derives the noise-prediction and flow-matching objectives these experts train on.

The decoder choice spans `{python} DecoderFamilies.spread_mult_str` in latency on the same backbone, the cost that parallel decoding and action experts were introduced to remove [@kim2025openvlaoft; @black2024pi0]. None of the four renews within the chunk policy's `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_period_str` period, because the prefill alone exceeds it. A large backbone that reads each observation fresh cannot also be the fast renewer on this processor, whatever its decoder. Deployed dual systems reach the same conclusion by assigning renewal to a separate, smaller model, as @tbl-03-state-of-practice records, and the machine does the same with its ACT chunk policy.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_decoder_family_latency_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of four horizontal bars for one fresh 16-step chunk: binned tokens 2.9 seconds, FAST tokens 899 milliseconds, parallel head 264 milliseconds, flow expert 241 milliseconds. A dotted line marks the shared prefill at 189 milliseconds and a red dashed line marks the 50 milliseconds renewal period, left of every bar."}

*No decoder renews within `{python} DecoderFamilies.t_period_str`; the prefill alone is too slow.*
:::

Two further points follow from the expert design. Its weights, hundreds of megabytes, far exceed the processor's on-chip caches, so each refinement step pays another off-chip transfer; a head small enough to stay resident would change that term, and the processor's cache capacity decides whether it can. Reducing the number of refinement steps shortens the decoder, provided the proposals keep the required task quality, but it does not touch the prefill of a fresh observation.

Whatever the decoder, chunking creates one more problem, **chunk seam continuity**\index{Chunk seam continuity!jerk}. Because each action chunk is generated independently from rolling sensory observations, the tail of chunk $k$ and the head of chunk $k+1$ may exhibit slight positional and velocity discrepancies. If a controller concatenated these chunks directly, the resulting step-discontinuities in acceleration would inject large jerk ($\dddot{\mathbf{q}}$) into the physical linkages, inducing mechanical shock, acoustic vibration, gear-tooth wear, and motor overcurrent faults.

To reduce discontinuities between overlapping chunks, systems can implement **temporal ensembling**\index{Temporal ensembling!trajectory smoothing}, blending overlapping trajectory predictions via exponentially weighted averaging:

$$\mathbf{a}_t = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} w_k \, \mathbf{a}_t^{(k)}}{\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} w_k}, \quad w_k = \exp(-m \cdot k)$$

where $\mathbf{a}_t^{(k)}$ is the action for step $t$ predicted by the $k$-th oldest of the $n$ chunks that cover step $t$ ($k = 0$ is the oldest), and $m > 0$ is a tunable weighting rate. Following ACT, the oldest prediction receives the largest weight, which favors smoothness over responsiveness; a smaller $m$ lets new observations enter the blend faster [@zhao2023learning]. The formula assumes that the policy is queried at every control step, as ACT does, so that $n = \min(t + 1, \Horizon)$. The mobile manipulator's chunk policy renews every `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str` setpoints instead, and because its `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` renewal period is a whole number of `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str` steps, each new chunk starts on a setpoint boundary. The same formula then applies with $k$ counting renewals rather than steps. A `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str`-setpoint chunk renewed every `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str` setpoints gives at most $n =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_overlap_str` overlapping predictions at any step. A renewal period that fell between setpoints would leave each chunk's first action off the grid, and the blend would first have to interpolate every chunk onto common setpoint times. Below the proposal boundary, the permission path interpolates the admitted waypoints into a setpoint for every bus cycle, and the drives close their own velocity and current loops on those setpoints.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_action_chunk_windows_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Sequence strip of one action chunk of 16 steps at 25 ms each: the first two steps are already past when the chunk arrives, the next two run for 50 ms until the successor chunk takes over, and the remaining 12 are buffer that later chunks overlap."}

*Each chunk runs `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_per_renewal_str` of its `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str` steps; later chunks overlap the rest.*
:::

Ensembling has two limits. It averages, and the average of two valid predictions need not be valid: if an older chunk passes left of an obstacle and a newer one passes right, the blend steers between them [@black2025realtime]. It also ignores what executes while the policy computes. With the assumed `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_infer_str` inference and `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_str` setpoints, the arm consumes `{python} ChunkSchedule.n_frozen_str` setpoints of the previous chunk before the new one exists, so no new prediction can change them. *Real-time chunking*\index{Real-time chunking!committed prefix} treats those setpoints as committed. It freezes the part of the previous chunk that will execute during inference and has a flow or diffusion policy fill in the rest of the new chunk so that it agrees with that frozen prefix, rather than blending afterward [@black2025realtime]. The method arrives from the learning side at this chapter's distinction, in which the committed prefix is motion already admitted and the tail is a buffer that the next evaluation may still rewrite.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Temporal ensembling and real-time chunking at chunk seams are developed from the training side in @sec-training-action-chunking.
:::

::: {.callout-perspective title="The temporal ensembling jerk trap"}
Exponentially weighted temporal ensembling averages overlapping predictions, but averaging sampled setpoints alone guarantees neither continuous position nor continuous velocity between samples or at chunk boundaries. The interpolator on the permission path determines those properties. If successive chunks disagree in slope, a controller can receive a step in commanded velocity even when position remains continuous. In joint proportional-derivative (PD) tracking ($\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{K}_p \mathbf{e} + \mathbf{K}_d \dot{\mathbf{e}}$), that velocity jump produces a finite torque step. With an illustrative derivative gain for one joint, the diagonal entry $\PidDerivativeGain = 40\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\cdot\text{s/rad}$ of $\mathbf{K}_d$, and an illustrative velocity discontinuity $\Delta \dot{q} = 0.5\,\text{rad/s}$, the derivative term changes by $\Delta \tau = \PidDerivativeGain \Delta \dot{q} = 20\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. Dividing by the servo period would instead describe a torque slew rate, not a torque. Abrupt torque changes can excite mechanical resonances or exceed drive limits. Interpolation must match position, velocity, and acceleration at adjoining segments, the property called $C^2$ continuity, while enforcing the machine's velocity, acceleration, and torque limits. Smoothness alone does not establish that the requested motion is feasible.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The quintic spline that matches position, velocity, and acceleration across a chunk seam is developed in @sec-planning-quintic-splines.
:::

A chunked policy therefore has two rates that a single "action rate" conflates: the spacing of the waypoints it supplies and the interval between the fresh observations that change them. Supplying more waypoints from one sensory context does not refresh the observation on which they depend. A downstream controller can use current state measurements while tracking admitted waypoints between renewals, and its feedback corrects tracking errors within its capabilities, but a newly perceived obstacle still requires a timely checking or replanning response. The mobile manipulator's own budget makes this distinction quantitative, first for supply and then for the time the evidence behind a chunk stays true.

### Two proposers and the evidence horizon {#sec-brain-two-proposers}

Chunking reduces the cost per waypoint, but the decoder pricing showed that each fresh context still waits for the large backbone's prefill, whatever the decoder. The split that follows, a slow intent model above a fast chunk policy, can now be budgeted on the warehouse mobile manipulator, and the chunks the fast policy supplies can be checked against how long they stay true. Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking} applies the memory bound to the split and checks whether chunking alone could give the larger model the required renewal cadence.

Budgeting the split also needs a term that the stopping budget of @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline already charged, a lease, authority that lapses unless it is renewed\index{Lease!authority that lapses}. The motion the chunk policy proposes runs under a chunk lease\index{Chunk lease!proposer side}, the longest an admitted chunk may keep driving the actuators without an admitted successor, which @sec-nervous-lease-sizing sizes against the stopping budget. A renewal that arrives late is contained by that lease, not by the length of the chunk.

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-action-chunking-lpddr5
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEMORY WALL AND THE MACHINE'S TWO PROPOSERS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking and the
# │          memory-wall paragraphs that follow it
# │ Goal:    show why the mobile manipulator's intent model cannot renew a
# │          proposal every few tens of milliseconds while its chunk policy can
# │ Show:    98.0 ms per FP16 intent-model weight sweep (about 10 Hz before
# │          vision); 6.1 ms amortized weight-sweep time per setpoint over
# │          H = 16; 1.12 ms per chunk-policy sweep; intent 2 Hz with a computed
# │          336 ms INT4 latency (calc-brain-intent-model-latency); chunk policy
# │          20 Hz / 40 ms; renewal gap 6.7 periods; proposer weight traffic
# │          7 x 3.5 GB x 2 Hz + 0.16 GB x 20 Hz = 52.2 GB/s (37 percent)
# │ How:     t_stream = M_weights / (B_peak * dram_efficiency);
# │          tau_step = t_stream / H (calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization);
# │          bus share = (D M_int4 f_intent + M_chunk f_chunk) / B_sustained
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt,
    fmt_params,
    fmt_memory,
    fmt_bandwidth,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_time,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_display_math,
    check,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ActionChunkingLPDDR5:
    """Memory wall and action chunking amortization on the machine's application processor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    model = RM.intent_model  # category: chosen (the machine's intent model)
    chunk_model = RM.chunk_model  # category: chosen (the machine's chunk policy)
    soc = RM.brain_soc  # category: datasheet (application processor)
    params = model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    chunk_params = chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet
    bytes_per_param = 2 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; FP16 weight storage
    bytes_per_param_int4 = 0.5 * (byte / param)  # category: chosen; INT4 alternative
    b_peak = soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet
    soc_mem = soc.memory.capacity  # category: datasheet
    bus_efficiency = RM.dram_efficiency  # category: illustrative; sustained fraction of peak
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    intent_rate = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    intent_latency = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (calc_vla_inference_latency)
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision
    kv_layers = model.layers  # category: datasheet
    kv_hidden = model.hidden_dim  # category: datasheet
    kv_bytes = 2 * byte  # category: chosen; FP16 key and value storage
    cameras = 3  # category: illustrative; synchronized RGB streams
    patches_per_frame = 256  # category: derived; patch tokens per 224 x 224 frame at P = 14
    context_tokens = 800  # category: illustrative; visual plus language and proprioception tokens per step
    history_window = 5 * second  # category: illustrative; retained visual history
    history_rate = 10 * Hz  # category: illustrative; frames retained per second of history

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    weight_mem = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param)
    weight_mem_int4 = memory_from_params(params, bytes_per_param_int4)
    res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    b_sustained = res["b_sustained"]
    t_stream = res["t_stream"]
    f_single = res["f_single"]
    tau_step = res["tau_step"]
    chunk_span = (chunk_horizon * chunk_step).to(millisecond)

    chunk_weight_mem = memory_from_params(chunk_params, bytes_per_param)
    chunk_res = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=chunk_weight_mem,
        memory_bandwidth=b_peak,
        chunk_horizon=chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=bus_efficiency,
    )
    chunk_t_stream = chunk_res["t_stream"]

    # The renewal gap and the two proposers' share of the bus (weight traffic only).
    # The INT4 intent model streams its weights D times per evaluation: once under
    # the compute-bound prefill and once per remaining decode token (eq-brain-eval-latency).
    renewal_gap = (intent_latency * chunk_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    chunk_sweep_share = (chunk_t_stream * chunk_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    sweeps_per_eval = IntentModelLatency.d_action  # category: derived (1 + (D - 1) sweeps)
    intent_bw = (sweeps_per_eval * weight_mem_int4 * intent_rate).to(GB / second)
    chunk_bw = (chunk_weight_mem * chunk_rate).to(GB / second)
    proposer_bw = (intent_bw + chunk_bw).to(GB / second)
    proposer_share = (proposer_bw / b_sustained).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_decode_int4 = IntentModelLatency.int4["t_decode"].to(millisecond)
    decode_duty = (t_decode_int4 * intent_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    visual_tokens = cameras * patches_per_frame
    kv_per_token = (2 * kv_layers * kv_hidden * kv_bytes).to(MB)
    kv_per_frame = (kv_per_token * visual_tokens).to(MB)
    history_frames = round((history_window * history_rate).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    kv_history_visual = (kv_per_frame * history_frames).to(GB)
    kv_per_step = (kv_per_token * context_tokens).to(MB)
    kv_history = (kv_per_step * history_frames).to(GB)
    combined_mem = (weight_mem + kv_history).to(GB)
    combined_ratio = (combined_mem / soc_mem).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(weight_mem.to(GB).magnitude - 14.0) < 0.1, f"Unexpected weight footprint: {weight_mem}")
    check(abs(b_sustained.to(GB / second).magnitude - 142.80) < 0.05, f"Unexpected sustained bandwidth: {b_sustained}")
    check(abs(t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 98.04) < 0.005, f"Unexpected intent sweep: {t_stream}")
    check(abs(f_single.magnitude - 10.20) < 0.05, f"Unexpected single-sweep frequency: {f_single}")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Unexpected chunk horizon: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(tau_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 6.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected per-setpoint sweep time: {tau_step}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk span: {chunk_span}")  # 16 x 25 ms (M5)
    # 2026-09-28: ACT corrected to about 80M parameters (Zhao et al. 2023); intent
    # latency now computed from prefill plus decode (decision M2).
    check(abs(chunk_t_stream.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.1204) < 0.0005, f"Unexpected chunk sweep: {chunk_t_stream}")
    check(abs(intent_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected intent rate: {intent_rate}")
    check(abs(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Unexpected intent latency: {intent_latency}")
    check(intent_latency > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent model's evaluation must exceed the chunk period")
    check(abs(chunk_rate.to(ureg.hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk rate: {chunk_rate}")
    check(abs(chunk_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected chunk latency: {chunk_latency}")
    check(t_stream > (1 / chunk_rate), "The intent sweep alone must exceed the chunk period")
    check(weight_mem_int4 == RM.intent_weight_memory, "INT4 weights must match the deployed intent model")
    check(6.5 < renewal_gap < 7.0, f"Renewal gap drifted: {renewal_gap}")
    check(abs(intent_bw.magnitude - 49.0) < 1e-6 and abs(chunk_bw.magnitude - 3.2) < 1e-6, f"Proposer bandwidth drifted: {intent_bw}, {chunk_bw}")
    check(0.35 < proposer_share < 0.38, f"Proposer bus share drifted: {proposer_share}")
    check(0.25 < decode_duty < 0.35, f"Decode duty drifted: {decode_duty}")
    check(chunk_latency < (1 / chunk_rate), "The chunk policy's inference must fit its own period")
    check(kv_layers == 32 and kv_hidden == 4096, f"Unexpected intent-model shape: {kv_layers} x {kv_hidden}")
    check(visual_tokens == 768 and history_frames == 50, f"Unexpected KV scenario: {visual_tokens}, {history_frames}")
    check(abs(kv_per_token.magnitude - 0.524288) < 1e-9, f"Unexpected KV bytes per token: {kv_per_token}")
    check(abs(kv_history_visual.magnitude - 20.13) < 0.01, f"Unexpected visual KV history: {kv_history_visual}")
    check(abs(kv_history.magnitude - 20.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected context KV history: {kv_history}")
    check(abs(combined_mem.magnitude - 34.97) < 0.01, f"Unexpected weights plus KV footprint: {combined_mem}")
    check(0.45 < combined_ratio < 0.55, f"Weights plus KV must claim about half the SoC memory: {combined_ratio}")
    # margin_kv_history_memory_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 68.7 GB, 21 GB, 14 GB, 419 MB, and 0.52 MB.
    check(round(soc_mem.to(GB).magnitude, 1) == 68.7 and round(kv_per_step.magnitude) == 419, "KV ladder margin labels drifted")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(params, precision=0)
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
    bytes_per_param_str = fmt_int(bytes_per_param.magnitude)
    weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=0)
    weight_mem_int4_str = fmt_memory(weight_mem_int4, unit=GB, precision=1)
```
