```{python}
    chunk_weight_mem_str = fmt_memory(chunk_weight_mem, unit=GB, precision=2)
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    b_sustained_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_sustained, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    dram_eff_pct_str = fmt_percent(bus_efficiency, precision=0, style="prose")
    t_stream_ms_str = fmt_latency(t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    f_single_str = fmt_frequency(f_single, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=1)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_step_str = fmt_latency(tau_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    chunk_t_stream_str = fmt_latency(chunk_t_stream, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    intent_rate_str = fmt_frequency(intent_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    intent_latency_str = fmt_latency(round(intent_latency.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    kv_layers_str = fmt_int(kv_layers)
    kv_hidden_str = fmt_int(kv_hidden, commas=False)
    cameras_str = fmt_int(cameras)
    patches_per_frame_str = fmt_int(patches_per_frame)
    visual_tokens_str = fmt_int(visual_tokens)
    context_tokens_str = fmt_int(context_tokens)
    history_window_str = fmt_time(history_window, 'second', precision=0)
    history_rate_str = fmt_frequency(history_rate, unit=ureg.hertz, precision=0)
    kv_per_token_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_token, unit=MB, precision=2)
    kv_per_frame_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_frame, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_visual_str = fmt_memory(kv_history_visual, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_per_step_str = fmt_memory(kv_per_step, unit=MB, precision=1)
    kv_history_str = fmt_memory(kv_history, unit=GB, precision=1)
    combined_mem_str = fmt_memory(combined_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)
    soc_mem_gb_str = fmt_memory(soc_mem, unit=GB, precision=1)

    tau_step_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{amort}}}} = \frac{{t_{{\text{{stream}}}}}}{{H}} = \frac{{{t_stream_ms_str}}}{{{chunk_horizon_str}\text{{ setpoints}}}} \approx {tau_step_str}\text{{ per setpoint}}"
    )
    t_replan_str = fmt_latency((1 / chunk_rate).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_gap_str = fmt(renewal_gap, precision=1)
    chunk_sweep_share_str = fmt_percent(chunk_sweep_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    sweeps_per_eval_str = fmt_int(sweeps_per_eval)
    intent_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(intent_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    chunk_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(chunk_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    proposer_bw_str = fmt_bandwidth(proposer_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=1)
    proposer_share_str = fmt_percent(round(proposer_share, 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    t_decode_int4_str = fmt_latency(round(t_decode_int4.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    intent_period_str = fmt_latency((1 / intent_rate).to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    renewal_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{t_{{\text{{INT4}}}}}}{{T_{{\text{{replan}}}}}} = \frac{{{intent_latency_str}}}{{{t_replan_str}}} \approx {renewal_gap_str}\text{{ renewal periods}}, \qquad \frac{{{chunk_weight_mem_str}}}{{{b_sustained_str}}} \approx {chunk_t_stream_str}"
    )
    bus_display_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"S_{{\text{{out}}}}\,M_{{\text{{INT4}}}}\,f_{{\text{{intent}}}} + M_{{\text{{chunk}}}}\,f_{{\text{{chunk}}}} = {sweeps_per_eval_str} \times {weight_mem_int4_str} \times {intent_rate_str} + {chunk_weight_mem_str} \times {chunk_rate_str} = {intent_bw_str} + {chunk_bw_str} = {proposer_bw_str}"
    )
```

::: {#nbk-brain-lpddr5-memory-wall-bottleneck-action-chunking .callout-notebook title="The renewal gap"}

**Problem**: Chunking spreads one weight sweep across many setpoints. Can it let the intent model renew proposals within the chunk policy's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_replan_str` period, or does the machine need a second, smaller proposer, and how much of the shared bus do the two proposers then take?

**Variables**:

* Intent model: `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of FP16 or `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_int4_str` of INT4 weights (Derived), an INT4 evaluation of `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_latency_str` that decodes $\EmittedTokenCountOut =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.sweeps_per_eval_str` tokens (Derived, notebook \ref{nbk-brain-intent-model-latency}), run at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_rate_str` (Chosen).
* Chunk policy: `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_params_str` parameters, ACT's size (Datasheet), `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_weight_mem_str` in FP16 (Derived), renewed at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str` (Chosen).
* Chunk of $\Horizon =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_horizon_str` setpoints at $\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str` (Chosen); sustained bandwidth $\SustainedMemoryBandwidth =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.b_sustained_str` (Derived).

**Math**:

*Amortization.* Counting weight traffic only, as @sec-brain-action-chunking did, and setting aside the prefill's arithmetic and the other decode sweeps, one FP16 sweep that emitted a whole chunk would be shared by $\Horizon$ setpoints:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.tau_step_display_math`

*Renewal.* A fresh chunk still waits for a whole INT4 evaluation, prefill and decode together, while the chunk policy streams its own weights in about a millisecond; the rest of its inference target goes to vision encoding and the decoder's arithmetic:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.renewal_display_math`

*Bus share.* The INT4 intent model streams its weights $\EmittedTokenCountOut$ times per evaluation, once under the prefill and once per remaining token (@eq-brain-eval-latency); the chunk policy streams its weights once per renewal:
`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.bus_display_math`

**Result**: Amortization cuts the weight time per setpoint to `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.tau_step_str`, but each fresh intent-model chunk arrives `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.renewal_gap_str` renewal periods after its capture. The chunk policy's sweep takes `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_sweep_share_str` of its period. Together the two proposers average `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.proposer_bw_str` of weight traffic, `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.proposer_share_str` of the sustained bandwidth.

**Systems insight**: Amortization is a supply lever, not a renewal lever, so the machine renews with a second, smaller proposer. The average hides the timing. For `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.t_decode_int4_str` of every `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_period_str`, the intent model's decode sweeps are modeled at the full sustained bandwidth, so a chunk-policy evaluation that overlaps them competes for the same bus, and its latency target holds only if it is measured under that contention. A late renewal is not free: the arm keeps moving on the previous chunk, and the chunk lease bounds how far.

:::

The selected design follows. The `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy uses ACT as its size reference and is assumed to be adapted to the mobile manipulator. It proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str` (a `{python} ChunkSchedule.t_replan_str` replanning period), emitting waypoints spaced at $\Delta t =$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_step_str` (a `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_supply_str` supply rate), within a `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_latency_str` p99 inference target that includes vision, while the permission path interpolates admitted waypoints into per-cycle setpoints and the drives close their velocity and current loops at their own faster rates. The intent model revises its target at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.intent_rate_str`. That is a candidate architecture, not a measured timing result. Loaded execution must establish the inference target, and a percentile target still permits overruns; the chunk lease contains a missed renewal.

[What retained history would cost]{.heading-3-inline}
The intent model as deployed reads one frame and keeps nothing between evaluations, so the budget above is complete for it. A variant that conditioned on several seconds of history would add memory pressure that the weights alone do not show, and the cost is worth knowing before anyone proposes one. The per-token charge from @sec-brain-learned-representations, `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_token_str` of full-width FP16 keys and values across all `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_layers_str` layers through @eq-brain-kv-cache, now scales with history. One synchronized set of `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $224{\times}224$ frames (`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.cameras_str` $\times$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.patches_per_frame_str` $=$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.visual_tokens_str` patch tokens) adds `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_frame_str`. This is a standard multi-head attention estimate for a hypothetical multi-camera extension, not a measured cache footprint for the published OpenVLA checkpoint. Counting language and proprioception tokens along with the visual patches raises each step to $\SequenceLength \approx$ `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.context_tokens_str` tokens, so each observation step adds `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_per_step_str` of KV cache. Retaining an unpruned `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_window_str` historical context window at `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_rate_str` would yield `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.kv_history_str` of KV cache. This hypothetical history exceeds the published OpenVLA checkpoint's configured context window; the calculation exposes the storage cost of such an extension, rather than claiming that the checkpoint supports it. Combined with the intent model's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of weights, this example claims `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.combined_mem_str`, about half of the application processor's `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.soc_mem_gb_str` (the module sold as 64 GB counts in binary gigabytes, $64 \times 2^{30}$ bytes) before runtime overhead, memory that perception, mapping, and the chunk policy also need. Even where memory capacity permits, reading a large cache is further traffic on that same bus. Bounding retained history therefore serves both capacity and timely renewal. Spatial pooling or cross-attention can reduce context traffic; fixed-horizon action output does not by itself bound the observation history retained by the backbone.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_kv_history_memory_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale ladder of memory footprints: the processor's 68.7 GB, a 5-second retained history of 21 GB, the FP16 weights at 14 GB, one observation step at 419 MB, and one token at 0.52 MB."}

*`{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.history_window_str` of retained context outweighs the `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.weight_mem_str` of weights.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-conveyor-chunk-sizing
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONVEYOR CHUNK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-brain-conveyor-evidence-horizon in @sec-brain-two-proposers
# │ Goal:    size the chunk the mobile manipulator's arm executes against the
# │          mug's drift on the moving conveyor
# │ Show:    60 ms untracked deadline; the 219 ms tracked evidence horizon; the
# │          90 ms open-loop span (50 ms replanning period plus 40 ms
# │          inference) inside it; the 16-step, 400 ms chunk (25 ms steps
# │          since M5, 2026-09-28) as a supply buffer that would breach the
# │          grasp tolerance if executed to its end; half-rate sensitivity
# │          (140 ms, h_min = 6)
# │ How:     tau_ev = sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip) via MLSysIM
# │          calc_tracked_evidence_horizon (shared with Ch10); open-loop span, h_min, and
# │          chunk span from RM.chunk_schedule; drift = a_slip T^2 / 2
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_length, fmt_int, fmt_frequency, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class ConveyorChunkSizing:
    """Chunk supply and evidence horizon for the mug on the moving conveyor."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_conv = AISLE.v_conveyor  # category: illustrative
    a_slip = AISLE.a_conveyor_slip  # category: illustrative
    r_tol = AISLE.grasp_tolerance  # category: chosen
    e_0 = AISLE.grasp_initial_error  # category: illustrative
    chunk_rate = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    chunk_latency = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative
    chunk_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen
    chunk_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_ev = calc_tracked_evidence_horizon(r_tol, e_0, a_slip).to(millisecond)  # sqrt(2 (r_tol - e_0) / a_slip)
    sched = RM.chunk_schedule  # calc_chunk_renewal_schedule
    chunk_period = sched["renewal_period"]
    open_loop = sched["open_loop_span"]  # renewal period + inference
    h_min = sched["min_supply_setpoints"]  # ceil(open_loop / step)
    chunk_span = sched["chunk_span"]  # H x step
    drift_open_loop = (0.5 * a_slip * open_loop**2).to(millimeter)
    drift_full = (0.5 * a_slip * chunk_span**2).to(millimeter)
    margin = (r_tol - e_0).to(millimeter)
    t_untracked = (margin / v_conv).to(millisecond)  # freshness deadline e_max / v_max without tracking
    err_full = (e_0 + drift_full).to(millimeter)
    outlast = (chunk_span - tau_ev).to(millisecond)
    sched_half = calc_chunk_renewal_schedule(chunk_rate / 2, chunk_step, chunk_horizon, chunk_latency)  # sensitivity: half the renewal rate
    open_half = sched_half["open_loop_span"]
    h_min_half = sched_half["min_supply_setpoints"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_conv.to("m/s").magnitude - 0.20) < 1e-9, f"Conveyor speed drifted: {v_conv}")
    check(abs(tau_ev.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, f"Tracked evidence horizon drifted: {tau_ev}")
    check(abs(chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk period drifted: {chunk_period}")
    check(abs(open_loop.magnitude - 90.0) < 1e-9, f"Open-loop span drifted: {open_loop}")
    check(open_loop < tau_ev, "The open-loop span must sit inside the evidence horizon")
    check(h_min == 4, f"Minimum supply horizon drifted: {h_min}")
    check(h_min * chunk_step >= open_loop, "The minimum supply must bridge the open-loop span")
    check(chunk_horizon == 16, f"Chunk horizon drifted: {chunk_horizon}")
    check(abs(chunk_span.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk span drifted: {chunk_span}")
    check(chunk_span > tau_ev, "The full chunk must outlast the evidence horizon (buffer, not plan)")
    check(e_0 + drift_full > r_tol, "Executing the whole chunk open-loop must breach the grasp tolerance")
    check(
        abs(t_untracked.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6 and t_untracked < open_loop, "Untracked, the mug must leave tolerance before the first replacement"
    )
    check(open_half < tau_ev and h_min_half == 6, f"Half-rate sensitivity drifted: {open_half}, {h_min_half}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_conv_str = fmt_velocity(v_conv, unit="m/s", precision=2)
    a_slip_str = fmt_acceleration(a_slip, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(r_tol, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e_0_str = fmt_length(e_0, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    _tau_ev_rounded = round(tau_ev.magnitude) * millisecond  # whole-ms display; the guard pins 219.09 ms
    tau_ev_str = fmt_latency(_tau_ev_rounded, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_latency_str = fmt_latency(chunk_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    open_loop_str = fmt_latency(open_loop, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    h_min_str = fmt_int(h_min)
    chunk_horizon_str = fmt_int(chunk_horizon)
    chunk_step_str = fmt_latency(chunk_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_span_str = fmt_latency(chunk_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    drift_open_loop_str = fmt_length(drift_open_loop, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    drift_full_str = fmt_length(drift_full, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    margin_str = fmt_length(margin, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_untracked_str = fmt_latency(t_untracked, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    err_full_str = fmt_length(err_full, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    outlast_str = fmt_latency(round(outlast.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    chunk_rate_half_str = fmt_frequency(chunk_rate / 2, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    open_half_str = fmt_latency(open_half, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    h_min_half_str = fmt_int(h_min_half)

    # Display arithmetic for nbk-brain-conveyor-evidence-horizon (magnitudes, LaTeX units)
    _mm = fmt(margin.magnitude, precision=0)
    _v = fmt(v_conv.to("m/s").magnitude, precision=2)
    _a = fmt(a_slip.to("m/s**2").magnitude, precision=2)
    _ms = lambda q: fmt_int(round(q.to(millisecond).magnitude))  # whole-ms display; guards pin exact values
    untracked_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{r_{{\text{{tol}}}} - e_0}}{{v_{{\text{{conv}}}}}} = \frac{{{_mm}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{_v}\ \text{{m/s}}}} = {_ms(t_untracked)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    tau_ev_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{ev}}}} = \sqrt{{\frac{{2 \times {_mm}\ \text{{mm}}}}{{{_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2}}}} \approx {_ms(tau_ev)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    open_loop_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"T_{{\text{{replan}}}} + t_{{\text{{infer}}}} = {_ms(chunk_period)} + {_ms(chunk_latency)} = {_ms(open_loop)}\ \text{{ms}}, \quad \tfrac{{1}}{{2}} a_{{\text{{slip}}}} T^2 = \tfrac{{1}}{{2}} \times {_a} \times ({fmt(open_loop.to(second).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{s}})^2 \approx {fmt(drift_open_loop.magnitude, precision=1)}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad h_{{\min}} = \left\lceil \tfrac{{{_ms(open_loop)}}}{{{_ms(chunk_step)}}} \right\rceil = {h_min}"
    )
    full_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"H\,\Delta t_{{\text{{step}}}} = {chunk_horizon} \times {_ms(chunk_step)}\ \text{{ms}} = {_ms(chunk_span)}\ \text{{ms}}, \quad e_0 + \tfrac{{1}}{{2}} \times {_a} \times ({fmt(chunk_span.to(second).magnitude, precision=2)}\ \text{{s}})^2 = {fmt(e_0.to(millimeter).magnitude, precision=0)} + {fmt(drift_full.magnitude, precision=0)} = {fmt(err_full.magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{mm}} > {fmt(r_tol.to(millimeter).magnitude, precision=0)}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )

ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_rounded = ConveyorChunkSizing._tau_ev_rounded
```

The split fixes how often each proposer renews. The moving target fixes how long each renewal stays true. At the pick station the arm takes the mug from a moving conveyor, and a chunk is useful only while the mug stays within the grasp tolerance $\PositionalTaskTolerance$ of where the chunk's evidence placed it, starting from the handle estimate's initial error $\InitialTrackingError$. Untracked, the belt's steady speed $v_{\text{conv}}$ uses up the margin $\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError$ within the freshness deadline $\InitialAndCeilingError/\SpeedBound$ of @sec-body-measurement-freshness, here with $\InitialAndCeilingError = \PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError$ and $\SpeedBound = v_{\text{conv}}$. A tracker removes that steady motion. It is the memory stage of the pipeline, re-estimating the mug's position and velocity from each new frame, and a chunk computed from its estimate aims at where the mug will be if the belt keeps its speed. What that extrapolation cannot foresee is a change of speed after capture, the mug slipping on the belt at a residual acceleration $a_{\text{slip}}$. The chunk's setpoints were fixed at its capture, so later frames do not correct them, and a segment executed open-loop for a time $\Time$ drifts by $\tfrac{1}{2} a_{\text{slip}} T^2$. Setting that drift equal to the margin gives the **tracked evidence horizon**\index{Evidence horizon!definition}, the longest the evidence behind a chunk keeps the mug within tolerance, in @eq-brain-evidence-horizon:
$$\EvidenceHorizon = \sqrt{\frac{2\,(\PositionalTaskTolerance - \InitialTrackingError)}{a_{\text{slip}}}}$$ {#eq-brain-evidence-horizon}
At worst, a chunk is replaced one renewal period plus one inference after the capture it was computed from, the reaction latency $T_{\text{replan}} + \ProposerInferenceTime$ of @sec-brain-action-chunking. That span must fit inside $\EvidenceHorizon$, and the chunk must carry enough setpoints to bridge it, as @eq-brain-min-supply requires:
$$h_{\min} = \left\lceil \frac{T_{\text{replan}} + \ProposerInferenceTime}{\Delta t_{\text{step}}} \right\rceil$$ {#eq-brain-min-supply}
Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-conveyor-evidence-horizon} applies both to the machine's schedule.

::: {#nbk-brain-conveyor-evidence-horizon .callout-notebook title="Buffer, not permission"}

**Problem**: The chunk policy renews every `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str`, is assumed to need `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str` per evaluation, and emits `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_horizon_str` setpoints `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_step_str` apart. Does the schedule depend on tracking the mug, how many setpoints must a chunk carry, and how much of each chunk may the arm execute on the evidence behind it?

**Variables**:

* Conveyor speed $v_{\text{conv}} =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.v_conv_str` and residual slip acceleration $a_{\text{slip}} =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.a_slip_str` (Illustrative).
* Grasp tolerance $\PositionalTaskTolerance =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.r_tol_str` (Chosen) and initial handle error $\InitialTrackingError =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.e_0_str` (Illustrative), a margin of `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.margin_str`.
* Renewal period $T_{\text{replan}} =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str`, setpoint step $\Delta t_{\text{step}} =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_step_str`, and $\Horizon =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_horizon_str` (Chosen); inference $\ProposerInferenceTime =$ `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`, a p99 target that includes vision (Illustrative).

**Math**:

*Untracked deadline.* The belt alone uses up the margin in
`{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.untracked_math`

*Tracked horizon.* With the steady motion removed, @eq-brain-evidence-horizon gives
`{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_math`

*Age at replacement and supply.* @eq-brain-min-supply and the drift over the executed span give
`{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_math`

*The whole chunk.* Executed open-loop to its end, one chunk would carry the mug to
`{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.full_math`

*Sensitivity.* Renewing at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_rate_half_str` instead raises the age at replacement to `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_half_str`, still inside $\EvidenceHorizon$, and $h_{\min}$ to `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.h_min_half_str`.

**Result**: Untracked, the mug leaves tolerance after `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.t_untracked_str`, before the first replacement at `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str`, so this schedule depends on the tracker. Tracked, the evidence holds for about `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`: `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.h_min_str` setpoints bridge each renewal, and the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` executed from each observation drifts only `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.drift_open_loop_str`. The `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` chunk outlasts its evidence by `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.outlast_str`.

**Systems insight**: The chunk is sized for supply, not for execution. Its tail beyond $\EvidenceHorizon$ keeps setpoints flowing if a renewal slips, but it is not permission to finish the motion, because the drift it would carry the arm through cannot be taken back once the gripper closes on the wrong place. The permission path therefore ages each chunk's evidence against $\EvidenceHorizon$, and when renewal stops, the chunk lease, not the chunk length, bounds how far the arm may keep going.

:::

On one clock, the schedule looks like @fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon. Each chunk is in force for only `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` before its successor replaces it, so the arm stops executing motion computed from any one capture once that capture is `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` old, well inside the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` the evidence supports; the rest of the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` chunk is reserve. If the chunk policy overruns its inference target, the notebook's assumption no longer holds, and if renewal stops altogether, a further setpoint remains eligible only while both its evidence and the active chunk lease remain valid. Overlapping chunks and temporal ensembling blend the executed motion across each renewal.

::: {#fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Chunk supply against the evidence horizon**: Time runs from the capture that the first chunk is computed from. The chunk policy renews every `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_period_str` and needs `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str` per evaluation, so each chunk is in force for one renewal period and is replaced when its evidence is `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop_str` old. The first chunk predicts `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of setpoints, but the tracked mug stays within the grasp tolerance only for the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` evidence horizon; the hatched tail is supply that keeps the setpoint stream full if renewal slips, not permission to execute it." fig-alt="Timing strip with five lanes on a shared millisecond axis from 0 to about 440. Capture ticks every 50 milliseconds; inference bars 40 milliseconds long starting at each capture; a lane showing chunks 0 to 3 each in force for 50 milliseconds starting at 40; the first chunk's span from 40 to 440 split into an executed segment to 90, a segment labeled evidence still valid to a red dashed line at 219, and a hatched segment labeled buffer, not permission to 440; and setpoint ticks every 25 milliseconds. Brackets above mark the 25 millisecond step, the 50 millisecond renewal, and the 90 millisecond age at replacement."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-03-chunk-supply-horizon
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNK SUPPLY AGAINST THE EVIDENCE HORIZON (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-03-chunk-supply-horizon, after the conveyor chunk-sizing
# │          paragraphs in @sec-brain-two-proposers

# │          how much of it the evidence behind it still covers

# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

# ┌── 1. LOAD (from calc-brain-conveyor-chunk-sizing) ─────────────────────────
_strip = viz.chunk_renewal_strip(RM, evidence_horizon=ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev)

# ┌── 3. GUARD (the strip draws the same schedule the prose prints) ───────────
check(RM.chunk_schedule["open_loop_span"] == ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop, "Strip and prose disagree on the age at replacement.")
check(RM.chunk_schedule["chunk_span"] == ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span, "Strip and prose disagree on the chunk span.")
check(
    ConveyorChunkSizing.open_loop < ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev < ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span,
```

:::

Under the stated assumptions, the conveyor calculation supplies the quantities needed to connect cognition to physical permission. One chunk covers `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_span_str` of motion, a new chunk takes up to `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.chunk_latency_str`, and the evidence stays within the stated grasp tolerance for about `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str`. The Nervous System must combine these proposer limits with the body's measured limits to establish its handoff record. That requires more information than a trajectory tensor alone. Timely delivery and usable evidence bound how long a proposal can remain eligible; they do not establish that the proposed grasp was correct.

### Handing intent to the chunk policy {#sec-brain-proposer-interface}

```{python}
#| label: calc-brain-proposer-interface
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AGE OF THE INTENT MODEL'S TARGET ON ARRIVAL
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-brain-proposer-interface and @tbl-03-state-of-practice
# │ Goal:    show that a target pose from one intent evaluation is already
# │          older than the conveyor's tracked evidence horizon when it arrives
# │ Show:    336 ms evaluation > 219 ms tau_ev, so a tracker must renew the pose
# │ How:     IntentModelLatency.t_int4 against ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_params, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class ProposerInterface:
    """Age of the intent model's target pose against the tracked evidence horizon."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    t_intent = IntentModelLatency.t_int4  # category: derived (calc_vla_inference_latency)
    tau_ev = ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev  # category: derived (conveyor slip model)
    chunk_params = RM.chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet (ACT)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    age_ratio = (t_intent / tau_ev).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(t_intent > tau_ev, "The intent target must be staler on arrival than the evidence horizon")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    chunk_params_str = fmt_params(chunk_params, precision=0)
```

The split between a slow semantic model and a fast visuomotor policy is not peculiar to this machine. Helix runs a `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_params_str`-parameter vision-language model at `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_lo_num_str` to `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s2_hi_str` above an `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s1_params_str`-parameter policy at `{python} StateOfPractice.helix_s1_rate_str` [@figureai2025helix], and GR00T N1 runs its vision-language model at `{python} StateOfPractice.gr00t_s2_rate_str` above a flow-matching transformer at `{python} StateOfPractice.gr00t_s1_rate_str` [@bjorck2025gr00t]. @Tbl-03-state-of-practice collects these and other published designs. Their rates bracket the machine's own `{python} IntentModelLatency.rate_str` and `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_rate_str`. What separates them is less their rates than what the slow model hands the fast one, and that choice decides what the permission path can check.

Three kinds of interface are in use. The first is a *latent vector*. Helix's slow model passes a single continuous latent that conditions the fast policy [@figureai2025helix], and GR00T N1's policy attends to token embeddings taken from an intermediate layer of its vision-language model [@bjorck2025gr00t]. A latent is trained end to end, carries whatever the fast policy finds useful, and costs no decoding. The second is a *language subtask*. $\pi_{0.5}$ first predicts the next subtask as text and then generates actions conditioned on it [@black2025pi05], and the orchestrating model of Gemini Robotics 1.5 sends its action model natural-language step instructions [@geminirobotics2025gemini15]. The third is a *geometric target*: Gemini Robotics-ER predicts points, two- and three-dimensional boxes, trajectories, and grasps, each with coordinates in the scene [@geminirobotics2025].

The permission path can check only a claim it can compare with its own evidence, and the three interfaces differ exactly there. A latent vector means something only to the network that reads it. No independent checker can tell whether it refers to the mug or to the photograph of a mug on a carton (@sec-brain-semantic-hallucinations), and it carries no position that could age against the evidence horizon $\EvidenceHorizon$. A text subtask can be checked against the task predicates the permission path has admitted, but "pick up the mug" names no location, so it can be neither compared with measured depth nor aged against drift. A geometric target allows both checks. It can be compared with calibrated depth and keep-out geometry, and aged from the capture time of the frame it came from. Only this interface lets an intent lease be enforced, because an intent lease names a grounded target, never a path, and expires at the earliest of the time its evidence stays valid and the deadlines the permission path sets. With a latent or a text interface, the permission path can still check each chunk's motion under the chunk lease, but the intent behind that motion goes unchecked.

The mobile manipulator therefore has its intent model emit a target: a position, an orientation, and a gripper command, the same seven values OpenVLA decodes as a step of motion, together with the capture time of the frame it read. The timing shows why that target cannot stand alone. One evaluation takes `{python} IntentModelLatency.total_int4_str`, longer than the `{python} ConveyorChunkSizing.tau_ev_str` tracked evidence horizon of the conveyor pick, so the pose the intent model read is stale before its target arrives. The intent model therefore contributes which object to take and approximately where, and the tracker of @sec-brain-two-proposers supplies where that object is now. The tracker binds the target to its own latest estimate of the mug, and the `{python} ProposerInterface.chunk_params_str`-parameter chunk policy aims at that fresh pose. The two leases then age against different clocks. The intent lease ages from the capture time of the tracker's latest estimate and is renewed each time the tracker confirms the same mug, so it lapses when tracking is lost or a permission-path deadline passes. Each chunk carries the capture time of the oldest observation behind it, normally the frame the chunk policy itself read, and its evidence ages from that time against $\EvidenceHorizon$.

The geometric bottleneck costs capability. A target pose cannot say how to fold a shirt or where to regrasp a cable, information a latent carries without a schema, so a checkable interface limits the tasks a single target can express. The machine accepts that limit in exchange for an intent the permission path can refuse. The same reasoning applies one level down to the chunk policy's action space. Joint targets can be checked directly against joint limits and end-effector poses against workspace keep-out regions, which is why the proposal payload of @sec-brain-proposer-information carries both.

### Information the proposer must supply {#sec-brain-proposer-information}

The conveyor budget gives each payload field a physical purpose. The receiver needs the candidate motion, the capture time from which its evidence ages, and the conditions limiting its validity. The following illustration groups that information with delivery metadata; it is not a new evidence record in the book's record chain. @Sec-nervous-supervisory-timers wraps this payload in the proposal header the permission path validates, and the Nervous System's handoff record combines this supply with the body's limits.

The **proposal payload**\index{Proposal payload!definition}\index{Proposal contract!definition}\index{Proposal boundary!contract schema} $\mathcal{P}$ is the typed candidate motion that the unprivileged Brain sends to the real-time Nervous System, packaged with the capture time of its evidence, the time after which it lapses, and the provenance the receiver needs to check it:
$$\mathcal{P} = \langle t_{\text{capture}}, t_{\text{valid}}, \Horizon, \Delta t, \mathbf{Q}_{1:\Horizon}, \dot{\mathbf{Q}}_{1:\Horizon}, \mathbf{X}_{1:\Horizon}, \mathbf{g}_{1:\Horizon}, \text{model\_id}, \text{lease\_id}, \hat{p}, \text{crc} \rangle$$
The capture and validity times let the receiver compare the motion with freshness and calibration requirements it establishes independently; for the conveyor pick, $t_{\text{valid}}$ can lie no later than $t_{\text{capture}} + \EvidenceHorizon$. The payload requests motion. It is neither execution permission nor the handoff evidence record, and a payload that omits its observation time or validity horizon invites the receiver to execute a proposal computed from a scene that no longer exists.

The fields in @tbl-03-proposal-record-schema illustrate the information needed to interpret a candidate trajectory, rather than prescribing a second wire format. The proposer supplies trajectory and observation information. Validity claims require supporting evidence, while the receiver applies the separately established chunk lease. A `lease_id` associates the request with that permission process; it does not let the proposer grant itself authority. The header and handoff record specify delivery, admission, and expiration.

| Field         | Type                        | Unit                    | Systems Semantics and Verification Rule                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|:--------------|:----------------------------|:------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `t_capture`   | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Hardware timestamp of oldest sensory observation conditioning the proposal.                                                                                                                                                     |
| `t_valid`     | `uint64_t`                  | $\text{ns}$             | Monotonic time after which proposal expires ($\le t_{\text{capture}} + \EvidenceHorizon$).                                                                                                                                      |
| `horizon_H`   | `uint16_t`                  | count                   | Number of prospective trajectory setpoints ($\Horizon =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.horizon_str` on this machine).                                                                                                                 |
| `delta_t`     | `uint32_t`                  | $\mu\text{s}$           | Temporal interval between consecutive waypoints ($\Delta t =$ `{python} ChunkSchedule.step_us_str` $\mu\text{s}$, a `{python} ChunkSchedule.f_supply_str` supply rate).                                                         |
| `q_traj`      | `float32[H][n]`             | $\text{rad}$            | Candidate joint trajectory array across $n$ degrees of freedom.                                                                                                                                                                 |

## Cognitive Vulnerabilities {#sec-brain-cognitive-vulnerabilities}

A chunk proposed by a mobile manipulator's policy can arrive within its `{python} ActionChunkingLPDDR5.chunk_latency_str` execution budget, with every joint setpoint smooth and within kinematic limits, and yet still collide the gripper into the rim of the mug. The trajectory meets its real-time deadline, but its physical content is wrong, and the most consequential failures of learned physical AI systems sit in that gap. Learned foundation models expand task coverage across open-world environments, but no general proof of their integrated, closed-loop behavior across unconstrained state spaces is available. Engineering practice must instead analyze verified components within explicitly bounded operating regions.

Without a verified input domain and sensitivity bound, small sensing changes to a learned proposer can yield unexpectedly large changes in proposed motion, a sensitivity demonstrated early by imperceptible image perturbations that flipped image classification outputs [@szegedy2013intriguing]. Benchmark success does not establish closed-loop stability, timing bounds, or physical safety under unseen operating conditions; those guarantees require independent evidence across the model, the software runtime, and the physical plant.[^fn-math-lipschitz-calibration] Even when a valid sensitivity bound exists, it characterizes only the relationship between input perturbations and output deviations over a specified domain. It provides no proof that the nominal proposed action is collision-free or physically admissible, meaning analytical bounds can inform, but never replace, an independent permission decision.

[^fn-math-lipschitz-calibration]: **Lipschitz Continuity in Neural Policies**\index{Lipschitz continuity!policy sensitivity}\index{Adversarial vulnerability!perturbation bounds}: Although neural networks with smooth activations are continuous on compact domains, a bound $L_{\text{lip}} = \sup_{\MechanicalPlantState_1 \ne \MechanicalPlantState_2} \frac{\lVert \pi(\MechanicalPlantState_1) - \pi(\MechanicalPlantState_2) \rVert}{\lVert \MechanicalPlantState_1 - \MechanicalPlantState_2 \rVert}$ must be established over a specified operating domain. If a valid bound exists, sensor error $\lVert \delta \MechanicalPlantState \rVert \le \epsilon$ implies $\lVert \delta \mathbf{a} \rVert \le L_{\text{lip}}\epsilon$; an unverified $L_{\text{lip}}$ supplies no usable action-error guarantee. Mathematical formulations appear in @sec-appendix-ml-lipschitz.

A numerical interface easily traps malformed tensors, NaN values, and out-of-range floating-point setpoints, but it cannot detect an erroneous grasp plan. Both classical deterministic pipelines and learned models can emit well-formed yet incorrect commands; learning, however, introduces failure modes rooted in high-dimensional latent representations, out-of-distribution hallucinations, and ungrounded model confidence. Independent safety monitors can reject proposals that contradict qualified geometry or physical joint limits, but they cannot deduce true task-level intent. Operating safely in physical environments requires examining these cognitive failure modes systematically and establishing the evidentiary contracts needed beyond basic packet validity.

### Semantic hallucinations {#sec-brain-semantic-hallucinations}

Consider a mobile manipulator clearing items near a conveyor. A discarded shipping carton carries a high-resolution printed photograph of a ceramic mug. The robot's vision backbone attends to the visual texture, and the policy proposes an end-effector trajectory that closes the parallel jaws around the printed handle. Numerically, the trajectory tensor is flawless: it is smooth, satisfies joint velocity and acceleration bounds, and avoids modeled obstacles. Yet the physical affordance it targets does not exist. In web-scale vision models, semantic attention maps reflect statistical correlations across two-dimensional pixel arrays rather than verified three-dimensional metric occupancy.

Independent geometric evidence can directly expose this hallucination. A runtime validator compares the proposed grasp geometry against calibrated depth telemetry, evaluating whether observed physical relief supports the object affordance. If the depth sensor reveals a planar cardboard surface within measurement resolution, the runtime rejects the proposal; if sensor dropouts or occlusions leave the region ambiguous, the proposal remains unverified and execution must pause. In neither case can a 2D attention map serve as a metric measurement of physical volume. The proposer must therefore expose both its target coordinate frame and the supporting observation timestamps, allowing downstream supervisory layers to distinguish a physically grounded motion plan from an unverified perceptual hypothesis.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How depth error is bounded and qualified before a spatial claim can be trusted is developed in @sec-perception-error-clearance.
:::

### The softmax illusion and out-of-distribution overconfidence {#sec-brain-softmax-illusion}

Deployment interfaces frequently conflate mathematical normalization with the physical probability of task success. In discrete classification, classification-based tokenization, or categorical action heads, raw output logits are transformed via the softmax operator:[^fn-softmax-function-origin]
$$\sigma(\mathbf{z})_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}$$
whose outputs sum to one purely by algebraic construction. When an embodied machine encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) observations, such as novel visual textures, intense specular glare, dynamic shadows, or water droplets on camera lenses, the network can still emit confidence scores near one for physically disastrous actions. Modern deep networks are often overconfident even on in-distribution inputs [@guo2017calibration], and networks constructed from rectified linear units provably approach maximum confidence on inputs far from their training distribution [@hein2019relu].

[^fn-softmax-function-origin]: **Softmax** (soft arg max): @bridle1990probabilistic named the normalized exponential "softmax" because it is a differentiable version of the winner-take-all operation that picks the largest input. A function built to pick a winner keeps doing so far from its training data, pushing its top output toward one whenever one logit separates from the rest, whether or not the input resembles anything the model has seen. \index{Softmax normalization!origin}\index{Probability calibration!algebraic normalization}

Calibration evaluates how closely a model's predicted confidence aligns with observed empirical success rates under specified conditions. A confidence score is useful for selecting or abstaining from a proposal only to the extent that this relationship holds for the deployed task. @Sec-appendix-ml-calibration formalizes binned expected calibration error and post-hoc temperature scaling. From a systems perspective, the execution runtime must bind calibration metadata directly to the model identity (`model_id`), preventing supervisory layers from mistaking uncalibrated algebraic certainty for physical permission.

In modern physical AI systems, populating the action payload's `confidence` field is rarely as straightforward as extracting a softmax probability, because contemporary chunking policies do not operate as discrete classifiers. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), for example, decodes each multi-step chunk deterministically at inference time by clamping its latent style variable to the prior mean [@zhao2023learning]. Similarly, diffusion and flow-matching policies iteratively denoise trajectories from Gaussian noise vectors. Neither architecture natively emits a normalized score. For these continuous decoders, confidence must be derived through an explicit, qualified estimation technique. Three primary architectures are used in practice:

* *Sample dispersion.* The system draws multiple trajectory chunks for the identical sensory observation by varying random diffusion noise seeds or sampling latent vectors. Measuring geometric dispersion across these trajectories describes the policy’s sampled output variability. Wide dispersion can reflect several valid motions as well as uncertainty; it does not by itself isolate uncertainty caused by missing knowledge.
* *Ensemble disagreement.* Multiple independently trained policy heads evaluate the same sensory input simultaneously. Downstream monitors measure the variance among their trajectory proposals, treating significant disagreement as an indicator of model uncertainty.
* *Conformal thresholds.* To convert heuristic dispersion or disagreement metrics into actionable statistical guarantees, the runtime applies inductive conformal prediction. Using a held-out calibration dataset, the system establishes an empirical threshold such that, under the assumption of exchangeability,[^fn-exchangeability-conformal-drift] the predicted set covers the calibrated target with a chosen marginal coverage probability. Physical validity still requires independent checks against current geometry and plant limits. If the conformal set is empty or contains mutually conflicting actions, the robot halts or solicits operator intervention [@ren2023robots; @angelopoulos2023gentle].

[^fn-exchangeability-conformal-drift]: **Exchangeability**\index{Exchangeability!conformal guarantee}: The conformal guarantee assumes only that the calibration trials and the new trial are exchangeable, a weaker condition than independent and identically distributed data [@vovk2005algorithmic]. A deployed robot can break even that weaker assumption because its actions change the scenes it meets next, the endogenous data of the second law (@sec-boundary-bedrock-laws). A threshold calibrated under one policy therefore has to be re-established after every policy or deployment change, and its stated coverage lapses in between.

Each uncertainty estimation strategy incurs distinct hardware and memory-bandwidth costs. Generating multiple samples from a single observation can reuse visual backbone features and batch each decoding iteration through the policy head, sharing a weight read across samples. Iterative decoders still revisit their weights across refinement steps, and the balance between arithmetic and memory traffic depends on the batch and kernels. In contrast, an ensemble of disparate models requires reading separate sets of weights across the memory bus for every head, multiplying memory bandwidth traffic by the number of heads. The action payload must therefore treat the confidence scalar $\hat{p}$ as meaningful only when accompanied by the identifier of the method that produced it and the corresponding calibration record, both resolved through `model_id`. A model lacking a qualified estimation pipeline must omit the confidence score entirely rather than emit an ungrounded default value.

The stipulated data in @tbl-03-calibration-degradation illustrate how environmental and hardware shifts induce severe overconfidence mismatches in practice (these values represent nominal illustrative regimes rather than a single deployed benchmark). Across all shifted regimes, reported confidence significantly outstrips actual task success. A supervisory filter relying solely on an uncalibrated score threshold would mistakenly admit hazardous trajectories. Choosing an appropriate supervisory response depends on the integrity of the remaining sensor streams and the physical capabilities of the machine; a confidence discrepancy alone cannot dictate whether the robot should slow down, collect additional sensor frames, or execute an emergency stop.

| Distribution Shift Regime               | Physical & Environmental Trigger                                             | Conf. vs. Success ($\text{conf} \text{ vs. } \text{success}$) | Confidence–Success Gap ($\text{conf}-\text{acc}$) | Downstream Supervisory Action                                                     |
|:----------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **In-Distribution** (Nominal Baseline)  | Clean optics, structured laboratory lighting, nominal workpiece textures     | $\text{conf}=0.91, \, \text{acc}=0.89$                        | $+0.02$                                           | Apply independent limits before nominal execution                                 |
| **Near-OOD Shift** (Covariate Shift)    | Specular reflections, lens water droplets, dynamic shadow transitions        | $\text{conf}=0.89, \, \text{acc}=0.52$                        | $+0.37$                                           | Abstain or seek new evidence; permit probing only with a qualified contact policy |
| **Far-OOD Shift** (Semantic Shift)      | Uncataloged deformable obstacles, human limb intrusion into workspace        | $\text{conf}=0.78, \, \text{acc}=0.08$                        | $+0.70$                                           | Reject proposal; use feasible controlled response                                 |
| **Sensor Degradation** (Hardware Drift) | Photodetector thermal noise ($>75^\circ\text{C}$), focal blur from vibration | $\text{conf}=0.84, \, \text{acc}=0.31$                        | $+0.53$                                           | Restrict operation to modes supported despite the sensor degradation              |

: **Illustrative Confidence–Success gaps under distribution shift**: Stipulated confidence and task-success rates for four operating regimes, with candidate responses requiring separate physical justification. These values are illustrative, not test results. {#tbl-03-calibration-degradation tbl-colwidths="[18,18,20,24,20]"}

### Perceptual chattering and covariate shift {#sec-brain-perceptual-chattering}

When sensory observations hover near decision boundaries between competing latent classes or grasp modes, subtle frame-to-frame sensor noise causes rapid classification toggling, a phenomenon known as *perceptual chattering*. If an unprivileged motion planner interprets each semantic flip as an instantaneous mutation in the physical world state, it continuously discards and resets its trajectory optimization. In the fatal 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle collision, the National Transportation Safety Board record documents this failure mode in the automated driving system: the perception subsystem alternated between classifying a pedestrian pushing a bicycle as a vehicle, a bicycle, and "other." After each reclassification the path predictor omitted the object's earlier locations, preventing the motion planner from recognizing that the obstacle was crossing the vehicle's path [@ntsb2019uber].\index{Perceptual chattering!state reset hazard}

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The tracking-history loss under classification changes in the 2018 Tempe collision is established in @sec-boundary-tracking-churn.
:::

In robotic manipulation, perceptual chattering can inject rapid, high-frequency direction reversals into joint trajectory setpoints. Over a discrete control interval $\Delta t$, a sharp step in commanded velocity implies an instantaneous acceleration demand $\Delta \dot{\mathbf{q}} / \Delta t$ that easily exceeds actuator capabilities. PD joint controllers react to the resulting velocity errors by commanding large, opposing motor torques, the same derivative-gain torque step that the temporal ensembling jerk trap of @sec-brain-action-chunking priced at a single chunk seam, now repeated at every flip. The resulting current spikes, tracking errors, and thermal stress strain the power stage and mechanical transmission, risking protective drive faults or structural vibration. Robust physical AI runtimes mitigate perceptual chattering using three complementary architectural mechanisms:

1. *Temporal hysteresis and debouncing.* Demanding that a newly observed semantic class or spatial mode persist across $N$ consecutive perception frames before committing an internal state transition, mirroring the debouncing[^fn-debounce-filter-latency] logic of embedded firmware.
2. *Recursive evidence accumulation.* Fusing successive observations into a persistent estimate, so that a transient, single-frame anomaly cannot abruptly overwrite an established world state.
3. *Kinematic rate and jerk limiting.* Enforcing strict joint-level acceleration and jerk boundaries at the real-time controller tier, ensuring that high-level semantic flickering cannot manifest as high-frequency torque shocks at the motor shafts.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Recursive state estimation, which accumulates evidence across frames instead of trusting the latest one, is developed in @sec-perception-state-estimation.
:::

[^fn-debounce-filter-latency]: **Debouncing**\index{Debouncing!latency cost}: The contacts of a mechanical switch bounce for milliseconds when pressed, so embedded firmware accepts a new switch state only after it has persisted for a set interval. The same $N$-frame rule applied to class labels suppresses chattering, but it delays every genuine change by $N$ frames, time charged to the observation-age budget before any proposal is renewed.

### Temporal expiration of intent {#sec-brain-temporal-expiration-intent}

Notebook \ref{nbk-brain-conveyor-evidence-horizon} already showed a chunk outliving its evidence, and the same failure applies one level up, to intent. Renewing a high-level goal identifier, or retransmitting a previous trajectory, does not refresh the observation that placed the mug. High-capacity intent models, which deliberate over long time horizons at low update rates, must therefore provide goals whose validity can be continuously audited against fresh, real-time telemetry while high-frequency reactive policies stream immediate motion.

The execution receiver must distinguish between rejecting a stale proposal and terminating an active, executing trajectory. Dropping an incoming proposal that failed its arrival deadline or validity check does not automatically invalidate the chunk currently running on the motors. The active chunk continues executing so long as its own chunk lease, the evidence behind it, its state bounds, and its safety margins all remain valid. Only when the active lease expires, or the evidence behind the active chunk lapses, without a valid successor must the supervisory permission path trigger an orderly fallback. Because holding position, decelerating to a controlled stop, and removing torque require distinct physical preconditions, @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder develops the formal fallback ladder across these operational regimes.

Each of the four vulnerabilities ends the same way. Hallucination, overconfidence, chattering, and expiry cannot be reliably ruled out by the proposer’s own output and require checks against independently qualified evidence, which is why the opening comparison of classical and learned methods resolves into a partition rather than a choice. Physical AI architectures assign semantic interpretation to the learned proposer and execution authority to the permission path. @Tbl-03-classical-vs-learned contrasts these paradigms. Learned foundation models supply flexible task coverage across unstructured environments, but their lack of closed-loop formal guarantees requires treating their outputs as unprivileged proposals. Conversely, classical analytical checks enforce strict physical invariances and real-time bounds, yet their guarantees remain conditional on accurate kinematic models and fresh sensor data. Safe embodied intelligence arises not from trusting the neural policy, but from structuring the interface so that unverified cognition can never bypass deterministic physics.

| Systems Dimension                 | Classical Analytical Methods                                                                       | Learned Foundation Models                                                                   | Physical AI Architectural Synthesis                                                   |
|:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Foundational Principle**        | Analytical differential equations, geometry, CAD models, Lyapunov stability                        | High-capacity neural representations fitted to empirical multimodal data                    | **Hybrid Hierarchy:** Learned intent proposals gated by the permission path           |
| **Generalizability & Perception** | **Model-dependent:** Explicit geometry and features may lose coverage under shift                  | **Data-dependent:** Open-vocabulary grounding can improve coverage but may fail under shift | **Unprivileged Deliberation:** Foundation models synthesize continuous semantic goals |
| **Mathematical Verifiability**    | **Conditional:** Selected properties can be proved within model assumptions                        | **Limited:** Empirical behavior needs separate bounds and runtime evidence                  | **Proposal Boundary:** Gate checks modeled limits using independent evidence          |
| **Temporal Pacing**               | **Boundable:** Selected controllers support real-time deadlines under stated execution assumptions | **Multi-Rate:** Full inference, chunk refresh, and waypoint execution have distinct rates   | **Split Proposers:** A small chunk policy renews while the intent model revises goals |
| **Failure Modes & Fallback**      | Implementation defects; model mismatch; failure on uncataloged objects                             | Semantic hallucinations; out-of-distribution overconfidence; expired intent                 | **Conditional Fallback:** Reject detected violations and execute a feasible response  |

: **Classical analytical methods vs. learned foundation models**: Trade-offs across generalizability, verifiability, pacing, and fallback, with the synthesis that partitions proposal capability from execution authority. {#tbl-03-classical-vs-learned tbl-colwidths="[20,26,26,28]"}

A proposal can meet every deadline and still target the wrong thing, so the receiver needs evidence the proposer cannot supply about itself.
